blocks.html: In Physics 2 charge sat on small objects, and Coulomb's law treated each one as a point. Real charged things are spread out: charge along a wire, over a metal plate, through a block of plastic. To find their fields we will cut them into pieces so small that each piece is a point charge, and then add the pieces with an integral. First we need a way to say how much charge each piece holds.

A charge density says how tightly charge is packed: $$\lambda = \frac{dq}{d\ell}\ \ (\text{C/m}), \qquad \sigma = \frac{dq}{dA}\ \ (\text{C/m}^2), \qquad \rho = \frac{dq}{dV}\ \ (\text{C/m}^3).$$ A small piece carries $dq = \lambda\,d\ell$, $\sigma\,dA$ or $\rho\,dV$, and the total is $Q = \int dq$. When the charge is spread evenly, the density is just total over size: $\lambda = Q/L$, $\sigma = Q/A$, $\rho = Q/V$.

Coulomb's law only knows about points. A density lets us give every tiny piece its own charge, so each piece can use the point-charge law. Adding infinitely many tiny pieces is exactly what a definite integral does: $Q = \int \lambda\,dx$ is the limit of the sum $\sum \lambda(x_i)\,\Delta x$. It is the same idea as mass density, where a rope's mass is $\int (\text{kg/m})\,dx$.

blocks.html: Round objects need pieces shaped to match them. For a disk, use thin rings of radius $r$ and width $dr$: $dA = 2\pi r\,dr$. For a ball, use thin shells: $dV = 4\pi r^2\,dr$. Each ring or shell has one radius, so a density that depends on $r$ is constant across it.

blocks.title: A charged shell
blocks.q: A thin spherical shell of radius $5.0\ \text{cm}$ carries $6.0\ \text{nC}$ spread evenly over its surface. Find $\sigma$.
steps: The charge sits on a surface, so we want $\sigma$, in C/m².
The area of a sphere is $A = 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi(0.050\ \text{m})^2 = 0.0314\ \text{m²}$.

blocks.title: A rod that gets denser
blocks.q: A rod runs from $x = 0$ to $x = 0.50\ \text{m}$ with $\lambda(x) = bx$, where $b = 40\ \text{nC/m}^2$. How much charge does it carry?
steps: The density changes along the rod, so we cannot just multiply. A piece $dx$ at position $x$ carries $dq = bx\,dx$.
Sense check: the density runs from $0$ to $20\ \text{nC/m}$, an average of $10\ \text{nC/m}$ over $0.50\ \text{m}$, which is $5.0\ \text{nC}$.

blocks.html: Mixing up the densities. A charged spherical shell has its charge on a surface, so $\sigma = Q/(4\pi R^2)$; a uniformly charged ball has it through a volume, so $\rho = Q/(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3)$. Writing $Q/(4\pi R^2)$ for a ball, or $Q/(\pi R^2)$ for a sphere's surface, mixes them. Check with units: $\lambda L$, $\sigma A$ and $\rho V$ must each give coulombs, so $\lambda$ needs C/m, $\sigma$ C/m² and $\rho$ C/m³.

blocks.html: You know how to add the fields of several point charges: find each one's field at the point, then add them as vectors. A charged rod is the same problem with infinitely many charges. Cut it into pieces $dq = \lambda\,dx$ (charge densities), treat each piece as a point charge, and add the pieces with an integral.

Each piece makes $dE = \dfrac{k\,dq}{r^2}$, pointing away from the piece (for positive charge). Split it into components and integrate each one separately:
        $$E_x = \int dE_x, \qquad E_y = \int dE_y.$$
        Use symmetry first: components that cancel in mirror-image pairs integrate to zero.

An integral adds numbers, not arrows. Two arrows of size 3 at right angles add to 4.2, not 6. So we turn one vector sum into two ordinary sums, one per component, where plain addition is correct. The size $dE$ may be added directly only when every piece's field points the same way, as for a point on the rod's own line.

blocks.name: em-pieces

opts.task: Raise the number of pieces. Watch the sideways parts of mirror-image arrows cancel, and compare adding sizes with adding vectors.

blocks.cap: A $10\ \text{nC}$ rod $40\ \text{cm}$ long, with P $10\ \text{cm}$ above its middle. With more pieces the vector sum settles on the exact integral, $4020\ \text{N/C}$; adding the sizes stays about 24% too high.

items: Draw axes and one piece $dq$ at a general position, say $x$.
Write its distance $r$ to the point, and the angle or ratio that gives each component (for example $\cos\theta = d/r$).
Write $dE_x$ and $dE_y$ in terms of $x$ and $dx$.
Use symmetry to drop components that cancel.
Integrate over the whole object, then check a limit you know (far away, it must look like a point charge).

blocks.title: On the rod's own line
blocks.q: A rod $0.20\ \text{m}$ long carries $8.0\ \text{nC}$ spread evenly. Find the field at a point on the rod's line, $0.10\ \text{m}$ beyond one end.
steps: Put P at the origin and the rod from $x = a = 0.10\ \text{m}$ to $x = a + L = 0.30\ \text{m}$. Every piece pushes along the same line, so here the sizes may be added.
Check: far away ($a \gg L$) this is $kQ/a^2$, a point charge.
blocks.a: $E \approx 2400\ \text{N/C}$, along the rod's line, away from the rod

blocks.title: Above the middle
blocks.q: A rod $0.40\ \text{m}$ long carries $10\ \text{nC}$. Find the field $d = 0.10\ \text{m}$ above its midpoint.
steps: Rod from $x = -L/2$ to $L/2$, P at $(0, d)$. A piece at $x$ is $r = \sqrt{x^2 + d^2}$ away.
Mirror pieces at $\pm x$ cancel each other's $x$-parts. The $y$-part of each is $dE\cos\theta = \dfrac{k\lambda\,dx}{r^2}\cdot\dfrac{d}{r}$.

$$E = k\lambda d\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}\frac{dx}{(x^2 + d^2)^{3/2}}$$ With the substitution $x = d\tan\theta$, $dx = d\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$, the integrand becomes $\cos\theta\,d\theta/d^2$, so the antiderivative is $\dfrac{x}{d^2\sqrt{x^2 + d^2}}$.
$$E = \frac{(8.99 \times 10^{9})(10 \times 10^{-9})}{(0.10)\sqrt{0.010 + 0.040}} = 4020\ \text{N/C}$$ pointing straight away from the rod.

blocks.title: Two checks on the answer
blocks.q: Check the result $E = kQ/\left(d\sqrt{d^2 + L^2/4}\right)$ far away and very close.
steps: Far away, $d \gg L$: the square root is about $d$, so $E \approx kQ/d^2$. From far off, the rod looks like a point.
Very close, $d \ll L$: the root is about $L/2$, so $E \approx \dfrac{2kQ}{dL} = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{d}$. Up close, the rod looks endless. Gauss's law will give the same $2k\lambda/d$ in one line.
blocks.a: Both limits come out right, a good sign the integral is correct.

blocks.html: Adding the sizes $dE$. Integrating $k\lambda\,dx/r^2$ without the factor $d/r$ treats every piece's field as if it pointed straight up. For the second example that gives $\dfrac{2k\lambda}{d}\arctan\dfrac{L}{2d} = 4980\ \text{N/C}$, about 24% too big. The sideways parts point left and right and cancel; only the parts along the bisector survive. Quick check: unless every piece pushes along the same line, the true field is smaller than the sum of the sizes.
At a point that is not on a line of symmetry (above one end of the rod, say), nothing cancels. Then you must integrate both $dE_x$ and $dE_y$, and the field tilts away from the rod.

blocks.html: A ring is the friendliest charge distribution of all. For a point on its axis, every piece of the ring is the same distance away. That makes the integral from the charged rod almost free, and once we have the ring, a disk is just many rings.

Take P on the axis, a distance $z$ from the center. Every piece $dq$ is $r = \sqrt{z^2 + R^2}$ from P. Its field has a part along the axis, $dE\cdot\dfrac{z}{r}$, and a part sideways. The piece directly across the ring has an equal and opposite sideways part, so all the sideways parts cancel. The axial parts all point the same way, and since $z$ and $r$ are the same for every piece, they come straight out of the integral:
        $$E = \frac{z}{r}\cdot\frac{k}{r^2}\int dq = \frac{kQz}{(z^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}.$$

On the axis of a ring: $E = \dfrac{kQz}{(z^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}$. On the axis of a disk with surface density $\sigma$:
        $$E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2 + R^2}}\right).$$
        Both point along the axis, away from the object if it is positive.

blocks.name: em-pieces

opts.task: P starts at the center of the ring. Move it out along the axis and watch the field grow from zero, peak, then fade.

blocks.cap: At the center every piece's arrow has a partner pointing the opposite way: the sizes add to a lot, but the vectors add to zero.

blocks.title: A ring
blocks.q: A ring of radius $4.0\ \text{cm}$ carries $5.0\ \text{nC}$. Find the field on its axis $3.0\ \text{cm}$ from the center.

blocks.title: Where the ring's field peaks
blocks.q: Along the axis, where is the ring's field strongest?
steps: $E(z) \propto z(z^2 + R^2)^{-3/2}$. Differentiate with the product and chain rules: $$\frac{dE}{dz} \propto (z^2 + R^2)^{-3/2} - 3z^2(z^2 + R^2)^{-5/2}.$$
Set it to zero and multiply by $(z^2 + R^2)^{5/2}$: $z^2 + R^2 - 3z^2 = 0$, so $z = R/\sqrt{2}$.
For the $4.0\ \text{cm}$ ring, the peak is $2.8\ \text{cm}$ from the center. The field is zero at the center, rises to this peak, then falls off.

blocks.title: A disk, built from rings
blocks.q: A disk of radius $10\ \text{cm}$ carries $10\ \text{nC}$ spread evenly. Find the field on its axis $2.0\ \text{cm}$ from the center.
steps: A ring of radius $r$ and width $dr$ has $dq = \sigma\,2\pi r\,dr$ and gives $dE = \dfrac{kz\,\sigma\,2\pi r\,dr}{(z^2 + r^2)^{3/2}}$. All of these point the same way, along the axis.
With $u = z^2 + r^2$, $du = 2r\,dr$: $$E = k\sigma\pi z\int_{z^2}^{z^2 + R^2}u^{-3/2}\,du = 2\pi k\sigma\left(1 - \frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2 + R^2}}\right)$$ and $2\pi k = \dfrac{1}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

blocks.html: Two limits tell the story of the disk. Very close ($z \ll R$) the bracket is nearly 1 and $E \approx \sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$, the field of an endless sheet, the same at every small distance. Far away, a binomial expansion of the bracket gives $E \approx kQ/z^2$: the disk looks like a point.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: The ring's axial field against distance: zero at the center, a peak at $R/\sqrt{2}$, then a $1/z^2$ fall. Drag P along the axis.

blocks.html: "The field must be huge at the center of the ring, since the charge is so close." It is zero there. Every piece is close, but each one's push is cancelled by the piece across from it. Check with the formula: $z = 0$ makes $E = 0$. (The potential at the center is not zero; potentials are numbers that do not cancel, as you will see in potentials of charge distributions.)

blocks.html: In magnetic flux you counted how much magnetic field passes through a loop: $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$. Electric flux is the same idea for $\vec{E}$. It will be the key to Gauss's law, which turns hard field integrals into one-line answers.

Give each small patch of surface a vector $d\vec{A}$: its area, pointing along the patch's normal (perpendicular to the surface). Then $$\Phi_E = \int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}.$$ For a uniform field and a flat surface, $\Phi_E = EA\cos\theta$, with $\theta$ the angle between $\vec{E}$ and the normal. Units: N·m²/C. On a closed surface the normals point outward, so field leaving counts as positive and field entering as negative.

Only the part of $\vec{E}$ that crosses the surface carries anything through it; the part skimming along the surface carries nothing. The dot product $\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = E\,dA\cos\theta$ picks out exactly the crossing part. Think of rain and a window: held flat under the rain it catches the most, tilted it catches less, and held edge-on it catches none.

blocks.name: flux
blocks.cap: A uniform field straight up through a tilted disk. Tilt it: the flux falls as $\cos\theta$ of the tilt and reaches zero when the disk stands edge-on to the field.

blocks.title: A tilted square
blocks.q: A uniform field of $500\ \text{N/C}$ passes through a square $20\ \text{cm}$ on a side. The field makes a $30^\circ$ angle with the surface of the square. Find the flux.
steps: The formula needs the angle to the normal. The normal is $90^\circ$ from the surface, so $\theta = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$.

blocks.title: A field that changes across the surface
blocks.q: A field points along $+z$ with $E_z = cy$, $c = 200\ \text{N/(C·m)}$. Find the flux through the rectangle $0 \le x \le 0.30\ \text{m}$, $0 \le y \le 0.20\ \text{m}$ in the $xy$-plane.
steps: The field is not uniform, so integrate. Along a thin strip at height $y$ the field is constant, and the strip's area is $dA = (0.30)\,dy$. The field is along the normal, so $\cos\theta = 1$.

blocks.title: A closed box in a uniform field
blocks.q: A uniform field points along $+x$. What is the net flux out of a closed cube with its faces along the axes?
steps: On the face where the field enters, the outward normal points against the field: flux $-EA$.
On the opposite face the outward normal points along the field: flux $+EA$.
On the other four faces the field skims the surface: flux $0$. Total: $0$. Every line that goes in comes out.

blocks.html: Using the angle to the surface. In the first example, $\cos 30^\circ$ would give $17.3\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}$ instead of $10$. The formula's $\theta$ is measured from the normal. A quick check: when the field runs parallel to the surface, nothing passes through, so the flux must be zero; only the angle to the normal (then $90^\circ$) makes $\cos\theta = 0$.

blocks.html: Here is a surprising fact about electric flux. Put a point charge $q$ at the center of an imaginary sphere of radius $r$. The field on the sphere is $kq/r^2$, straight out through every patch, and the sphere's area is $4\pi r^2$. So the flux is $$\Phi_E = \frac{kq}{r^2}\cdot 4\pi r^2 = 4\pi k q = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}.$$ The radius dropped out. A bigger sphere has a weaker field over a larger area, and the two changes cancel exactly, because the field falls as $1/r^2$ and area grows as $r^2$.

Gauss's law: for any closed surface, $$\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0},$$ where $q_{\text{enc}}$ is the net charge inside. Charges outside the surface add nothing to the net flux.

Any shape: the field lines leaving a point charge are the same lines whether you surround it with a sphere, a cube or a potato; each line crosses the surface once on its way out, so every closed surface around the charge collects the same $q/\varepsilon_0$.
Charges outside: a line from an outside charge that enters the surface must leave it again. It adds negative flux where it enters and the same positive flux where it leaves. The field on the surface changes, but the total does not.
Many charges: fields add, so fluxes add: $\Phi = (q_1 + q_2 + \dots)/\varepsilon_0$ over the charges inside.

blocks.name: ph-efield

opts.task: Drag the dashed surface and change its size. The net flux changes only when a charge crosses the surface.

blocks.cap: A Gaussian surface (dashed) among three charges. Red arrows show field leaving the surface and blue ones field entering. Charges outside change the arrows but not the total.

blocks.title: Counting what is inside
blocks.q: A closed surface contains $q_1 = +4.0\ \text{nC}$ and $q_2 = -1.0\ \text{nC}$; $q_3 = +6.0\ \text{nC}$ sits just outside. Find the net flux.
steps: $q_3$ is close and strong, but its lines go in and come back out.

blocks.title: One face of a cube
blocks.q: A $12\ \text{nC}$ charge sits at the center of a cube. How much flux passes through one face?
steps: The whole cube gets $q/\varepsilon_0$. The six faces are identical as seen from the center, so they share it equally.

blocks.title: A charge at a corner
blocks.q: An $8.0\ \text{nC}$ charge sits exactly at one corner of a cube. How much flux passes out through the cube?
steps: Eight cubes meeting at that corner would surround the charge completely and share $q/\varepsilon_0$ equally.
So one cube gets $\dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0} = 113\ \text{N·m²/C}$. (The three faces touching the corner get none: the field skims along them.)

blocks.html: "A charge outside the surface changes the flux through it." It changes the field at points on the surface, sometimes a lot, but not the net flux: each of its lines enters and leaves. Check yourself with a surface that encloses no charge at all: its net flux is zero no matter what fields are around it.

Gauss's law is always true, but it gives you $E$ only when symmetry makes $E$ the same size on the whole surface (or on whole pieces of it). Spheres, long cylinders and flat sheets have that symmetry; the next two topics use it.

blocks.html: Gauss's law becomes a tool for finding fields when the charge is spherically symmetric: a point charge, a charged shell, a ball, or layers of these. Symmetry says the field points straight out (or in) and has the same size everywhere on a sphere centered on the charge. On such a sphere the flux integral is just $E$ times the area.

Draw a Gaussian sphere of radius $r$ through the point you care about. The field is radial and the same size all over it, so
        $$\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = E\,(4\pi r^2) = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E = \frac{k\,q_{\text{enc}}}{r^2}.$$
        Every problem in this topic comes down to one question: how much charge is inside radius $r$? Charge farther out than $r$ contributes nothing at radius $r$.

Shell of charge $Q$, radius $R$: $E = 0$ inside, $E = kQ/r^2$ outside.
Uniform ball: inside, only the fraction $r^3/R^3$ is enclosed, so $E = \dfrac{kQr}{R^3}$, growing in step with $r$; outside, $E = kQ/r^2$.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: A uniformly charged ball. Drag P from the center outward: the field grows linearly inside, peaks at the surface, then falls as $1/r^2$. The dashed circle is the Gaussian sphere through P.

blocks.title: Inside and outside a ball
blocks.q: A ball of radius $6.0\ \text{cm}$ holds $12\ \text{nC}$ spread evenly. Find the field $3.0\ \text{cm}$ and $12\ \text{cm}$ from the center.
steps: At the surface both formulas give the same value, $kQ/R^2 = 3.00 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N/C}$, so the field is continuous there.

blocks.title: A charge inside a charged shell
blocks.q: A $+3.0\ \text{nC}$ point charge sits at the center of a thin shell of radius $5.0\ \text{cm}$ carrying $-5.0\ \text{nC}$. Find the field at $3.0\ \text{cm}$ and at $10\ \text{cm}$.
steps: At $3.0\ \text{cm}$ the Gaussian sphere encloses only the point charge: $E = \dfrac{(8.99 \times 10^{9})(3.0 \times 10^{-9})}{(0.030)^2} = 3.00 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N/C}$, outward.

At $10\ \text{cm}$ it encloses $3.0 - 5.0 = -2.0\ \text{nC}$: $E = \dfrac{(8.99 \times 10^{9})(2.0 \times 10^{-9})}{(0.10)^2} = 1800\ \text{N/C}$, pointing inward because the enclosed charge is negative.

blocks.title: A density that grows outward
blocks.q: A ball of radius $R = 10\ \text{cm}$ has $\rho = \rho_0 r/R$ with $\rho_0 = 20\ \mu\text{C/m}^3$. Find $E$ at $r = 5.0\ \text{cm}$.
steps: Enclosed charge, by thin shells: $$q(r) = \int_0^r \rho_0\frac{s}{R}\,4\pi s^2\,ds = \frac{\pi\rho_0 r^4}{R}$$
Gauss: $E(4\pi r^2) = \dfrac{\pi\rho_0 r^4}{\varepsilon_0 R}$, so $E = \dfrac{\rho_0 r^2}{4\varepsilon_0 R}$.

blocks.html: "The field inside a charged ball is zero, like inside a shell." A shell has no charge inside it, so a Gaussian sphere there encloses nothing. A ball has charge all the way in, so the enclosed charge, and the field, grow as you move out: $E = kQr/R^3$. Only at the very center is $E = 0$. Check with the first example: halfway out, the field is half the surface value, not zero.

blocks.html: Gauss's law also handles two other shapes with strong symmetry: a very long line (or cylinder) of charge and a very large flat sheet. The trick is choosing a Gaussian surface whose pieces either catch the field head-on or not at all.

Line: by symmetry the field points straight out from the line and depends only on the distance $r$. Wrap the line in a Gaussian cylinder of radius $r$ and length $\ell$. The flat ends get no flux (the field skims them); the curved side gets $E\cdot 2\pi r\ell$. It encloses $\lambda\ell$: $$E\,(2\pi r\ell) = \frac{\lambda\ell}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}.$$ Sheet: the field points straight away from the sheet on both sides. Use a pillbox through the sheet with caps of area $A$. Only the caps get flux, $2EA$, and it encloses $\sigma A$: $$2EA = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}.$$

Long line: $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, falling as $1/r$. Large sheet: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, the same at every distance. Inside a long uniform cylinder of radius $R$: $E = \dfrac{\rho r}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

blocks.cap: A large charged sheet: drag P away from it. The graph of $E$ against distance stays flat.

blocks.title: A long wire
blocks.q: A long wire carries $5.0\ \text{nC/m}$. Find the field $4.0\ \text{cm}$ away.
steps: This matches the close-up limit $2k\lambda/d$ of the rod integral, with far less work.

blocks.title: A large sheet
blocks.q: A large sheet carries $4.0\ \text{nC/m}^2$. Find the field $1.0\ \text{cm}$ and $5.0\ \text{cm}$ from it.
steps: The distance never entered, so it is the same at both points (as long as we are close compared with the sheet's size).

blocks.title: Two sheets: a capacitor
blocks.q: Two large parallel sheets carry $+4.0$ and $-4.0\ \text{nC/m}^2$. Find the field between them and outside them.
steps: Each sheet makes $226\ \text{N/C}$ on both sides: away from the positive sheet, toward the negative one.
Between the sheets both point the same way: $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0 = 452\ \text{N/C}$.
Outside, they point opposite ways and cancel: $E = 0$. This is the uniform field of a parallel-plate capacitor.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: A long line of charge: the field falls as $1/r$, more slowly than a point charge's $1/r^2$.

blocks.html: "A sheet's field gets weaker as you move away." For a sheet that is large compared with your distance, it does not. As you back away, each piece of the sheet is farther, but more of the sheet's pieces push in your direction rather than sideways, and the two effects cancel exactly. Check the formula: $\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$ has no distance in it. (A real sheet of size $D$ behaves this way only while you are much closer than $D$; far away it looks like a point.)

blocks.html: A metal is full of electrons free to move. Put extra charge on it, or hold it in a field, and those electrons rearrange within a tiny fraction of a second, then stop. That final, still state is electrostatic equilibrium. With Gauss's law and the pillbox, three facts about it follow quickly.

In a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium:
1. $E = 0$ everywhere inside the metal.
2. Any excess charge sits on the surface.
3. Just outside, $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to the surface, with $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$.

1: if there were a field inside, the free electrons would feel a force and move. "Nothing moves" therefore means $E = 0$.
2: draw a Gaussian surface anywhere inside the metal, just under the surface. $E = 0$ on it, so its flux is zero and it encloses zero net charge. The excess has nowhere to be but the surface.
3: a field along the surface would push charges along it, so the outside field must be perpendicular. A tiny pillbox with one cap outside and one inside the metal gets flux only through the outer cap: $EA = \sigma A/\varepsilon_0$. That is twice a lone sheet's $\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$, because here all the field goes out one side.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: A charged metal sphere. The charge spreads over the surface, the field inside is zero, and outside it is $kQ/r^2$ with lines leaving the surface at right angles. Change the charge with the slider.

blocks.title: Field from surface charge
blocks.q: A flat part of a charged metal plate has $\sigma = 20\ \text{nC/m}^2$. Find the field just outside.

blocks.title: A charge in a cavity
blocks.q: A $+3.0\ \text{nC}$ point charge sits at the center of a hollow metal shell that carries net charge $-5.0\ \text{nC}$. How is the shell's charge divided between its inner and outer surfaces?
steps: Draw a Gaussian sphere inside the metal. $E = 0$ there, so it encloses zero net charge: the inner surface must carry $-3.0\ \text{nC}$ to cancel the point charge.
The shell's total is $-5.0\ \text{nC}$, so the outer surface carries $-5.0 - (-3.0) = -2.0\ \text{nC}$.

blocks.title: Fields in each region
blocks.q: Same setup, with the shell's inner radius $5.0\ \text{cm}$ and outer radius $8.0\ \text{cm}$. Find the field at $3.0$, $6.0$ and $12\ \text{cm}$.
steps: At $3.0\ \text{cm}$ (in the cavity): only the point charge is enclosed, $E = kq/r^2 = 3.00 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N/C}$, outward.

blocks.html: "Extra charge spreads through the whole inside of a solid metal ball." In an insulator charge can stay where you put it, but in a metal it cannot: like charges push each other until every bit of excess sits on the outer surface. Check with Gauss's law: any surface drawn inside the metal has $E = 0$ on it, so it encloses no net charge.

Fact 1 also means a closed metal box shields its inside from static fields outside: charges on the box's surface rearrange until the field inside the metal, and in the empty space within, is zero. This is the idea behind a Faraday cage.

blocks.html: In Physics 2 potential was energy per charge, and near a point charge $V = kq/r$. That formula did not come from nowhere: it comes from the field by an integral. Once you know how, you can find the potential of anything whose field you know, including every field from Gauss's law.

$$V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$$ In a uniform field, along a straight step of length $d$ at angle $\theta$ to the field: $\Delta V = -Ed\cos\theta$. For charges of limited size we usually set $V = 0$ far away, so $V(P) = -\int_\infty^P \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$. Potential falls along the direction of the field.

Move a test charge $q$ a small step $d\vec{\ell}$. The field does work $q\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ on it, so its potential energy changes by $dU = -q\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ (energy the field gives away is energy the arrangement loses). Divide by $q$: $dV = -\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$. Add the steps from A to B with an integral, using the Fundamental Theorem when the field has an antiderivative. The electrostatic field is conservative, like gravity, so every path from A to B gives the same answer; pick the easiest one.

blocks.name: ph-graph
blocks.cap: The field of a $0.10\ \text{nC}$ point charge, $E = 900/r^2$ in N/C. The shaded area under $E(r)$ from A to B is the drop in potential, $V_A - V_B$. Drag the limits to see how the area changes.

blocks.title: A uniform field
blocks.q: A uniform field of $400\ \text{N/C}$ points along $+x$. Point B is $25\ \text{cm}$ from A, in a direction $60^\circ$ from the field. Find $V_B - V_A$.
steps: For a straight step in a uniform field, $\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ is the same all along: $\Delta V = -Ed\cos\theta$.
Only the part of the step along the field counts: $0.25\cos 60^\circ = 0.125\ \text{m}$. A step straight across the field would change nothing.

blocks.title: From a point charge's field
blocks.q: Find $V_B - V_A$ for a $5.0\ \text{nC}$ point charge, with A $2.0\ \text{cm}$ and B $6.0\ \text{cm}$ from it. Then find $V(r)$ itself.
steps: Walk outward along a radius, where $\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}\,dr$: $$V_B - V_A = -\int_{r_A}^{r_B}\frac{kq}{r^2}\,dr = kq\left(\frac{1}{r_B} - \frac{1}{r_A}\right)$$
Now let A go to infinity, where $V = 0$: $V(r) = kq/r$, the formula from Physics 2.

blocks.title: The center of a charged ball
blocks.q: A ball of radius $R$ holds charge $Q$ spread evenly. Taking $V = 0$ far away, find the potential at its center.
steps: Come in from infinity in two stretches. Outside, the field is $kQ/r^2$, so at the surface $V(R) = kQ/R$.
Inside, $E = kQr/R^3$ (from Gauss's law), so $$V(0) - V(R) = -\int_R^0 \frac{kQr}{R^3}\,dr = \frac{kQ}{2R}$$
$V(0) = \dfrac{kQ}{R} + \dfrac{kQ}{2R} = \dfrac{3kQ}{2R}$. The center is where $E = 0$, yet $V$ is highest there: zero field means $V$ is flat, not zero.

blocks.html: Dropping the minus sign. Without it, potential would rise as you move along the field, so a positive charge would be at the bottom of its own hill. Check with a positive point charge: its field points away from it and its potential $kq/r$ falls as you move away. Moving with the field must lower $V$.
For an infinitely long line of charge the integral from infinity diverges, so only differences make sense: $V_B - V_A = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac{r_B}{r_A}$.

blocks.html: For rings and disks we added field vectors piece by piece and had to watch every component. Potential is kinder. Each piece $dq$ contributes $k\,dq/r$, a plain number with no direction, and numbers just add. This is often the easiest road to the field too: find $V$ first, then take its slope.

With $V = 0$ far away,
        $$V = \int \frac{k\,dq}{r}.$$
        Ring, on its axis: $V = \dfrac{kQ}{\sqrt{z^2 + R^2}}$. Disk, on its axis: $V = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{z^2 + R^2} - z\right)$. Rod, on its own line, $a$ beyond the end: $V = k\lambda\ln\dfrac{a + L}{a}$.

Each piece $dq$ is a point charge, and a point charge's potential is $k\,dq/r$. Potentials of several charges add because their fields add: $-\int(\vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2)\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ splits into two integrals. Since each term is a number (positive for positive charge), there is no cancelling by direction and no need for components.

blocks.name: em-pieces

opts.task: Each bar is one piece's k Δq/r. Move P and change the number of pieces.

blocks.cap: Potential from a ring, piece by piece. Every bar counts fully; nothing cancels, even at the center, where the field is zero.

blocks.title: A ring, at the center and on the axis
blocks.q: A ring of radius $5.0\ \text{cm}$ carries $4.0\ \text{nC}$. Find $V$ at its center and on its axis $12\ \text{cm}$ from the center.
steps: At the center every piece is $R$ away: $V = \dfrac{kQ}{R} = \dfrac{(8.99 \times 10^{9})(4.0 \times 10^{-9})}{0.050} = 719\ \text{V}$.
On the axis every piece is $\sqrt{z^2 + R^2} = \sqrt{0.12^2 + 0.05^2} = 0.13\ \text{m}$ away: $V = \dfrac{kQ}{0.13} = 277\ \text{V}$.

blocks.title: A rod, on its own line
blocks.q: A rod $0.30\ \text{m}$ long carries $6.0\ \text{nC}$. Find $V$ at a point on its line, $0.10\ \text{m}$ beyond one end.

blocks.title: A disk, from rings
blocks.q: A disk of radius $10\ \text{cm}$ carries $10\ \text{nC}$ spread evenly. Find $V$ on its axis $5.0\ \text{cm}$ from the center.
steps: A ring of radius $r$, width $dr$ holds $dq = \sigma\,2\pi r\,dr$ and adds $\dfrac{k\,dq}{\sqrt{z^2 + r^2}}$.

$$V = k\sigma\pi\int_0^R\frac{2r\,dr}{\sqrt{z^2 + r^2}} = 2\pi k\sigma\left(\sqrt{z^2 + R^2} - z\right) = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{z^2 + R^2} - z\right)$$ (substitute $u = z^2 + r^2$).

items: Charge with strong symmetry (sphere, long line, big sheet): find $\vec{E}$ with Gauss's law, then integrate it to get $V$.
Charge without that symmetry (ring, disk, finite rod): add $k\,dq/r$ directly. It is a single ordinary integral, with no angles.
Need the field too? Find $V$ along a line, then differentiate: the field is minus the slope of the potential.

blocks.html: Splitting potential into components. Writing $dV\cos\theta$, or cancelling the potentials of pieces on opposite sides, treats $V$ like a vector. It is not: a ring's center has $V = kQ/R$ even though the field there is zero, and that stays true if the charge is bunched on one side. Check: does every term in your sum have the sign of its own charge, with no angles in it? Then you are adding potentials correctly.

blocks.html: Integrating the field gives the potential. Running that backward, the field is the slope of the potential. In three dimensions "slope" means the gradient, built from partial derivatives. This is often the fastest way to a field: find the scalar $V$ (no components), then differentiate.

$$E_x = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \quad E_y = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial y}, \quad E_z = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial z}, \qquad \text{that is}\quad \vec{E} = -\nabla V.$$
        For a potential that depends only on $r$: $E_r = -dV/dr$. The field points downhill in $V$, at right angles to the equipotentials, and is strongest where they crowd together.

Take a tiny step $d\ell$ in some direction. From $dV = -\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$, the component of $\vec{E}$ along the step is $-dV/d\ell$. Step along $x$ and you get $E_x = -\partial V/\partial x$; the same for $y$ and $z$. Stepping along an equipotential changes nothing, so the field has no component along it: field lines cross equipotentials at right angles.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: A dipole with its equipotentials (dashed). Field lines cross them at right angles and are densest where the equipotentials crowd. The black dashed line, $V = 0$, runs between the charges, where the field is strong.

blocks.html: Think of a hiking map. The equipotentials are the contour lines, $V$ is the height, and $\vec{E}$ points straight downhill, steepest where the contours bunch up. A conductor in equilibrium has $E = 0$ inside, so the whole conductor sits at one potential and its surface is an equipotential. That is why field lines always meet a metal surface at right angles.

blocks.title: One dimension
blocks.q: Along the $x$-axis, $V(x) = 5x^2 - 3x + 2$ (volts, $x$ in meters). Find $E_x$ at $x = 1.0\ \text{m}$.
steps: At $x = 1.0$: $E_x = -(10 - 3) = -7\ \text{V/m}$. The field points along $-x$, toward lower $V$.

blocks.title: Three dimensions
blocks.q: $V = 2x^2y - 3yz + 4z$ (volts, meters). Find $\vec{E}$ at $(1, 2, -1)$.
steps: $\partial V/\partial x = 4xy$, $\partial V/\partial y = 2x^2 - 3z$, $\partial V/\partial z = -3y + 4$.

blocks.title: The ring, the easy way
blocks.q: On a ring's axis $V = kQ/\sqrt{z^2 + R^2}$. Find $E_z$.
steps: $E_z = \dfrac{kQz}{(z^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}$: the same result as adding field vectors, with no components to track.

blocks.html: "Where $V = 0$, the field must be zero too." The field depends on how fast $V$ changes, not on its value. Midway between $+q$ and $-q$, $V = 0$ but the potential is dropping steeply from the positive charge toward the negative one, so $E$ is large there. The reverse happens inside a charged metal sphere: $V$ is not zero but it is flat, so $E = 0$. Check: look at the slope, never the height.

blocks.html: Two charges store potential energy $U = kq_1q_2/r$: positive if they repel, negative if they attract. What about three charges, or a dozen? The energy of the whole group is the work it takes to assemble it, bringing the charges in from far away one at a time.

$$U = \sum_{\text{pairs } i < j}\frac{kq_iq_j}{r_{ij}}$$
        One term for each pair, counted once. $N$ charges make $N(N-1)/2$ pairs.

Assemble the charges one at a time. The first costs nothing: no other charges are there yet. The second costs $kq_1q_2/r_{12}$. The third moves through the potential of the first two, costing $q_3(V_1 + V_2) = kq_1q_3/r_{13} + kq_2q_3/r_{23}$. Each new charge adds one term for each charge already present, so in the end every pair appears exactly once. The order of assembly does not matter; the total is the same.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: Three charges, three pairs. Drag them: pulling the attracting pair apart takes work, pushing the repelling pairs together takes work too.

blocks.html: This energy belongs to the arrangement as a whole, not to any one charge. Its sign tells a story. Positive $U$ means repulsion won while you built the group: let go, and the charges fly apart, turning $U$ into kinetic energy. Negative $U$ means attraction won: the group is bound, and you must supply $|U|$ to take it apart. The same bookkeeping explains why atoms and ionic crystals hold together.

blocks.title: Three in a line
blocks.q: Charges of $+3.0$, $-2.0$ and $+1.0\ \mu\text{C}$ sit in a line, $0.10\ \text{m}$ apart in that order. Find $U$.
steps: $U = -0.584\ \text{J}$. Negative: assembling them released energy, and pulling them apart would take that much work.

blocks.title: Four at the corners of a square
blocks.q: Four $2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ charges sit at the corners of a square with $0.10\ \text{m}$ sides. Find $U$.
steps: $4 \cdot 3/2 = 6$ pairs: four along the sides ($r = a$) and two across the diagonals ($r = a\sqrt{2}$).

blocks.title: Adding one more
blocks.q: How much work does it take to bring a fifth charge, $+1.0\ \mu\text{C}$, from far away to the center of that square?
steps: The work for the newcomer is its charge times the potential the others make there: $W = qV$. The energy among the first four does not change.
Each corner is $a/\sqrt{2} = 0.0707\ \text{m}$ from the center: $V = 4\cdot\dfrac{kq}{a/\sqrt{2}} = 1.02 \times 10^{6}\ \text{V}$.

blocks.html: Counting each pair twice, or skipping some. Summing $kq_iq_j/r_{ij}$ over every $i$ and every $j \ne i$ counts each pair twice and doubles $U$. Forgetting the diagonals of a square leaves pairs out. Check the number of terms: it must be $N(N-1)/2$, so 3 for three charges and 6 for four.

blocks.html: The electric force is conservative, like gravity, so a charge moving among fixed charges keeps its total energy: whatever potential energy it loses becomes kinetic energy. With potentials in hand, this is often the quickest way to find a speed: no forces, no accelerations, no time.

$$\Delta K + q\,\Delta V = 0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^2 = -q(V_f - V_i).$$ A positive charge speeds up moving to lower potential; a negative charge speeds up moving to higher potential. One electron-volt, $1\ \text{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$, is the energy an electron gains crossing $1\ \text{V}$.

The work the field does on the charge equals the drop in its potential energy, $-q\Delta V$, and by the work-energy theorem that work is $\Delta K$. Because the electrostatic force is conservative, the path does not matter, only the start and end potentials.

The electron-volt is handy because $q\,\Delta V$ is then just arithmetic: an electron crossing $500\ \text{V}$ gains $500\ \text{eV}$, and an alpha particle (charge $2e$) crossing the same $500\ \text{V}$ gains $1000\ \text{eV}$, whatever their masses. Convert to joules only when you need a speed. And remember that $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ is the slow-speed formula: when a speed comes out above about a tenth of the speed of light, relativity gives a noticeably different answer.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: An electron entering the gap between charged plates. The field does work on it; its kinetic energy grows by $e\,\Delta V$ as it moves toward the positive plate.

blocks.title: An electron gun
blocks.q: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through $500\ \text{V}$. How fast is it going?
steps: About 4% of the speed of light, so the classical formula is still fine.

blocks.title: Pushed away by a fixed charge
blocks.q: A proton is released from rest $2.0\ \text{mm}$ from a fixed $+5.0\ \text{nC}$ charge. How fast is it moving when it is far away?
steps: Far away the potential is zero, so the proton loses all of $U = \dfrac{kQe}{r}$: $$K = \frac{(8.99 \times 10^{9})(5.0 \times 10^{-9})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})}{0.0020} = 3.60 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{J}$$

blocks.title: Rutherford's closest approach
blocks.q: An alpha particle ($+2e$) with $5.0\ \text{MeV}$ of kinetic energy heads straight for a gold nucleus ($+79e$). How close does it get?
steps: At the turning point it is momentarily at rest, so all of its $K$ has become $U = \dfrac{k(2e)(79e)}{r}$.

$$r = \frac{(8.99 \times 10^{9})(2)(79)(1.60 \times 10^{-19})^2}{8.0 \times 10^{-13}} = 4.55 \times 10^{-14}\ \text{m}$$ about $45.5\ \text{fm}$. That is thousands of times smaller than a gold atom (radius about $1.4 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$), so the atom's positive charge must be packed into a tiny nucleus.

blocks.html: "Charges always speed up moving toward lower potential." That is true for positive charges only. For an electron, $\Delta K = -q\Delta V = +e\Delta V$: it gains energy moving toward higher potential, the way a bubble rises in water. Check with forces: the field points from high to low $V$, and a negative charge is pushed opposite the field, toward high $V$.

blocks.html: A conductor in equilibrium has no field inside, so every point of it is at the same potential (ΔV = −∫E·dl is zero along any path through the metal). Join two conductors with a wire and they become one conductor. Charge flows through the wire until the whole thing, both objects and the wire, sits at one potential.

Connected conductors reach the same potential. For two spheres far apart, $V = kQ/R$ for each, so $$\frac{Q_1}{R_1} = \frac{Q_2}{R_2}, \qquad Q_1 = Q_{\text{total}}\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}.$$ The charge divides in proportion to the radii, and the surface field $E = V/R$ is stronger on the smaller sphere.

While the potentials differ, there is a field along the wire, and that field pushes charge from the higher-potential sphere toward the lower one. The flow stops only when the potentials match. A sphere's potential is $kQ/R$: a big sphere can hold more charge at the same potential, because its charge is spread over a larger surface farther from the center. So equal potentials mean $Q \propto R$, not equal charges. At the surface, $E = kQ/R^2 = V/R$, so with $V$ shared, the small sphere's field is stronger.

blocks.name: em-share

opts.task: Connect the wire and watch the charge move. Then change the radii.

blocks.cap: Two metal spheres. With the wire connected, both reach the same potential; the charge splits in proportion to the radii, and the smaller sphere ends up with the stronger surface field.

blocks.title: Sharing with an empty sphere
blocks.q: A $2.0\ \text{cm}$ sphere holding $8.0\ \text{nC}$ is joined by a long wire to an uncharged $6.0\ \text{cm}$ sphere far away. Find the final charges, the potential and the surface fields.
steps: $E_1 = V/R_1 = 4.50 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N/C}$ and $E_2 = V/R_2 = 1.50 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N/C}$: three times stronger on the small sphere.

blocks.title: Both spheres charged
blocks.q: A $3.0\ \text{cm}$ sphere with $+10\ \text{nC}$ and a $5.0\ \text{cm}$ sphere with $-4.0\ \text{nC}$, far apart, are joined. How much charge flows through the wire?
steps: Charge is conserved: the total is $10 + (-4.0) = 6.0\ \text{nC}$.
Sphere 1 went from $10$ to $2.25\ \text{nC}$, so $7.75\ \text{nC}$ crossed the wire (in practice, electrons moved the other way).

blocks.html: "Connected spheres end up with equal charges." Equal charges would give the smaller sphere the higher potential ($kQ/R$ with a smaller $R$), and charge would keep flowing. What the wire equalizes is potential. Check your answer by computing $Q/R$ for both spheres: the two values must match.

The same reasoning explains why the field is strongest at sharp points of a charged conductor: a sharp tip behaves like a tiny sphere at the conductor's potential. That is how lightning rods and the needles in some air ionizers work, by concentrating the field at a point.

"Far apart" matters. If the spheres were close, each one's charge would change the other's potential, and the split would no longer follow the simple ratio of the radii. The potentials would still end up equal.

blocks.html: In Physics 2 you used $C = Q/V$ and the parallel-plate formula $C = \varepsilon_0 A/d$. Now we can derive capacitance for any shape that Gauss's law can handle, by finding the field and then integrating it into a voltage.

Put $+Q$ and $-Q$ on the two conductors, find $\vec{E}$ between them, integrate to get $\Delta V$, then $C = Q/\Delta V$.
        $$\text{plates: } \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}, \qquad \text{coaxial: } \frac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)}, \qquad \text{spheres: } 4\pi\varepsilon_0\frac{ab}{b - a}, \qquad \text{lone sphere: } 4\pi\varepsilon_0 R.$$

The field between the conductors is proportional to $Q$ (Gauss's law), so $\Delta V = \int E\,dr$ is proportional to $Q$ too. In the ratio $Q/\Delta V$ the charge cancels, leaving only sizes and $\varepsilon_0$. Capacitance is a property of the shape, like the volume of a bottle. A smaller gap or a bigger area means less voltage for the same charge, so more capacitance.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: A parallel-plate capacitor on a battery. Change the gap: $C$, and with it the charge, change, but $C$ never depends on the voltage.

blocks.title: Parallel plates
blocks.q: Plates of area $100\ \text{cm}^2$ sit $1.0\ \text{mm}$ apart in air. Find $C$.
steps: Between the plates $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0 = Q/(\varepsilon_0 A)$, uniform, so $\Delta V = Ed = Qd/(\varepsilon_0 A)$ and $C = \varepsilon_0 A/d$.

blocks.title: A coaxial cable
blocks.q: A coaxial cable $10\ \text{m}$ long has an inner conductor of radius $0.50\ \text{mm}$ and an outer conductor of radius $2.0\ \text{mm}$, with air between. Find $C$.
steps: With charge per length $\lambda = Q/L$ on the inner conductor, Gauss gives $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ between the conductors.
$\Delta V = \int_a^b \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\,dr = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac{b}{a}$, so $C = \dfrac{\lambda L}{\Delta V} = \dfrac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)}$.

blocks.title: Concentric spheres
blocks.q: An inner sphere of radius $4.0\ \text{cm}$ sits inside a shell of radius $5.0\ \text{cm}$. Find $C$, and compare with the inner sphere alone.
steps: Between them $E = kQ/r^2$, so $\Delta V = kQ\left(\dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{b}\right)$ and $C = \dfrac{ab}{k(b - a)} = 4\pi\varepsilon_0\dfrac{ab}{b - a}$.
Move the shell far away ($b \to \infty$): $C \to 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a = 4.45\ \text{pF}$. Bringing the second conductor close raises $C$ fivefold.

blocks.html: Notice the pattern in all four formulas: capacitance grows when the conductors are large and close together. Close conductors let a lot of charge sit at a small voltage, because the opposite charges nearly cancel each other's fields everywhere but in the thin gap. That is why real capacitors roll up long strips of foil separated by a very thin film. A lone conductor has surprisingly little capacitance: Earth itself, treated as an isolated sphere of radius $6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$, has only $4\pi\varepsilon_0 R \approx 709\ \text{μF}$, less than some capacitors that fit in your hand.

"Capacitance depends on the voltage applied." $C = Q/V$ looks as if more voltage means less capacitance, but $Q$ grows in step with $V$, and the ratio stays fixed. Check with the formulas above: none of them contains $V$ or $Q$. Doubling the battery voltage doubles the charge and leaves $C$ alone.

blocks.html: A charged capacitor stores energy $U = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$. But where is it? Not in the charges themselves, it turns out, but in the space between the plates, wherever there is electric field. That idea, that fields carry energy, is what lets light carry energy across empty space.

An electric field stores energy with density
        $$u = \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\quad(\text{J/m}^3),$$
        and the total is $U = \int u\,dV$ over all the space where the field is.

Take a parallel-plate capacitor: $C = \varepsilon_0 A/d$ and $V = Ed$. Then $$U = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}(Ed)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\,(Ad).$$ $Ad$ is the volume between the plates, the only place the field is. So the energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$ per cubic meter of field. The formula is general: it holds for any field, not just a capacitor's.

blocks.name: ph-efield
blocks.cap: An isolated capacitor. Widen the gap: the charge and the field stay the same, but there is more field-filled volume, so the stored energy grows. The work you do pulling the plates apart goes into that new field.

blocks.title: A strong field
blocks.q: Dry air breaks down at a field of roughly $3.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{V/m}$. How much energy is stored per cubic meter in a field that strong?
steps: About $40\ \text{J}$ per cubic meter: modest, which is one reason air-gap capacitors cannot store much energy.

blocks.title: Two ways to the same energy
blocks.q: A capacitor with $200\ \text{cm}^2$ plates $1.0\ \text{mm}$ apart is charged to $100\ \text{V}$. Find the stored energy from the field, then check it with $\tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$.

blocks.title: A charged sphere's field
blocks.q: A metal sphere of radius $R$ carries $Q$. Find the energy in its field, and how much of it lies within $2R$ of the center.
steps: Outside, $E = kQ/r^2$; inside the metal, $E = 0$. Shells of volume $4\pi r^2\,dr$ hold $u\,4\pi r^2\,dr$.

$$U = \int_R^\infty \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0\frac{k^2Q^2}{r^4}\,4\pi r^2\,dr = \frac{kQ^2}{2}\int_R^\infty\frac{dr}{r^2} = \frac{kQ^2}{2R}$$ (using $4\pi\varepsilon_0 k = 1$). That matches $\tfrac{1}{2}QV$ with $V = kQ/R$.
Stopping the integral at $2R$ gives $\dfrac{kQ^2}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{2R}\right)$: half the energy lies within one radius of the surface.

blocks.html: "The energy sits on the charges on the plates." For still charges both pictures give the same total, so it is easy to think the energy is in the charges. But fields can move away from their charges: a radio wave keeps carrying energy long after the antenna's charges have stopped. Check yourself with the isolated capacitor: pulling the plates apart changes neither charge, yet the energy grows, exactly in step with the volume of field.

blocks.html: Fill the gap of a capacitor with an insulator such as glass, plastic or oil, and its capacitance goes up by a factor $\kappa$, the material's dielectric constant. What else changes depends on one question: is the battery still connected?

A dielectric that fills the gap gives $C = \kappa C_0$.
Battery connected (fixed $V$): $Q \to \kappa Q_0$ and $U = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2 \to \kappa U_0$.
Isolated (fixed $Q$): $V \to V_0/\kappa$, $E \to E_0/\kappa$ and $U = Q^2/(2C) \to U_0/\kappa$.

An insulator has no free electrons, but its molecules can stretch or turn. In the field between the plates they line up a little, positive ends toward the negative plate. Inside the material these tiny dipoles cancel each other, but at the two faces a thin layer of bound charge is left over, opposite in sign to the nearby plate. That bound charge cancels part of the plates' field. With a weaker field for the same free charge, the voltage is smaller, and $C = Q/V$ is larger.

blocks.html: Current is charge per second through a wire. Inside a copper wire, what is actually moving, and how fast? The answer is surprising: the electrons creep along far more slowly than a snail, even though the lamp at the end of the wire lights the instant you flip the switch.

$$I = nqv_dA, \qquad J = \frac{I}{A} = nqv_d,$$ where $n$ is the number of free charges per cubic meter, $q$ the charge of each, $v_d$ their average drift velocity and $A$ the wire's cross section. $J$ (A/m²) is the current density.

Picture a cross section of the wire. In a time $\Delta t$, every carrier within a distance $v_d\Delta t$ upstream of it gets through. Those carriers fill a cylinder of volume $Av_d\Delta t$, which holds $nAv_d\Delta t$ of them (a number density, like the charge densities you met earlier). Each carries $q$, so $\Delta Q = nqAv_d\Delta t$, and dividing by $\Delta t$ gives $I = nqv_dA$.

The electrons are not sitting still otherwise: they zip about randomly at around $10^{6}\ \text{m/s}$, but in every direction at once, so the random part carries no net charge. The field adds a slow, steady drift on top.

blocks.html: "The electrons race through the wire at nearly the speed of light." What travels that fast is the field: when you close a switch, the push spreads along the wire in nanoseconds, and electrons everywhere in the circuit, including those already in the lamp, start drifting at once. Each electron creeps along at a fraction of a millimeter per second. Check with the numbers above: at $0.19\ \text{mm/s}$, an electron would take over an hour to cross a room.

blocks.html: The formula $R = \rho L/A$ assumes the same cross section all the way along. Real conductors are not always so tidy: a tapered probe, a cone-shaped contact, or a cable where current flows outward through the insulation. For those, cut the conductor into thin slices, find each slice's resistance, and add.

Slices that carry the current one after another are in series, so their resistances add:
        $$R = \int \frac{\rho\,dx}{A(x)}.$$
        $dx$ is a slice's thickness along the current and $A(x)$ its area across the current.

A thin slice is so thin that its area is nearly constant across it, so the ordinary formula works for it: $dR = \rho\,dx/A(x)$. The same current passes through every slice in turn, which is exactly what series means, and series resistances add. The sum of infinitely many thin slices is an integral, which substitution usually handles.

blocks.q: A nichrome conductor ($\rho = 1.1 \times 10^{-6}\ \Omega\cdot\text{m}$) is $20\ \text{cm}$ long; its radius grows evenly from $1.0\ \text{mm}$ to $3.0\ \text{mm}$. Find its resistance for current from end to end.
steps: The radius is $r(x) = r_1 + \dfrac{r_2 - r_1}{L}x$, so $dR = \dfrac{\rho\,dx}{\pi r(x)^2}$.

Substitute $u = r(x)$, $dx = \dfrac{L}{r_2 - r_1}du$: $$R = \frac{\rho L}{\pi(r_2 - r_1)}\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\frac{du}{u^2} = \frac{\rho L}{\pi(r_2 - r_1)}\cdot\frac{r_2 - r_1}{r_1r_2} = \frac{\rho L}{\pi r_1r_2}$$
Check: if $r_1 = r_2$ this becomes $\rho L/(\pi r^2)$, the familiar formula.

steps: Now the "slices" are thin cylindrical shells: thickness $dr$ along the current, area $2\pi rL$ across it, and the current crosses them in series.

blocks.html: The slices also tell you where the heat goes. With the same current through every slice, each one turns $I^2\,dR$ into heat, so the thin end, with the largest $dR$ per length, runs hottest. That is why a wire with a nick or a narrow neck heats up and fails right there, and why fuses are made with a deliberately thin section.

Using one area for the whole conductor. Taking the average radius, $2.0\ \text{mm}$, in the first example gives $\rho L/(\pi r_{\text{avg}}^2) = 0.0175\ \text{Ω}$, 25% too small. The thin end resists far more than the wide end, and $1/r^2$ punishes thinness more than an average can show. Check: your answer should depend on the area along the whole length, so an integral (or at least a slice-by-slice sum) must appear.

blocks.html: When a circuit has two batteries in different branches, you cannot reduce it to one equivalent resistor. Instead you use Kirchhoff's two rules, which you met in Physics 2, to write one equation per unknown current, and solve them together, as in systems in three variables.

Junction rule: the current into a junction equals the current out. Loop rule: around any closed loop, the changes in potential add to zero.
Guess a direction for each branch current and keep it. If a current comes out negative, it flows the other way; the sign is part of the answer.

The junction rule is conservation of charge: in a steady current, charge cannot pile up at a junction. The loop rule says potential is a property of a place: walk around a loop and you are back where you started, at the same potential, so the rises and drops must cancel.

blocks.html: In Physics 2 you learned that a capacitor charges through a resistor with a time constant $\tau = RC$. Now we can see where the exponential comes from: the loop rule turns into a differential equation that separates neatly.

Close the switch at $t = 0$ with the capacitor empty. Around the loop: $\varepsilon - IR - \dfrac{q}{C} = 0$. The current is the rate the capacitor's charge grows, $I = dq/dt$, so
        $$R\frac{dq}{dt} = \varepsilon - \frac{q}{C} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dq}{C\varepsilon - q} = \frac{dt}{RC}.$$
        Integrate from $q = 0$ at $t = 0$: $-\ln\dfrac{C\varepsilon - q}{C\varepsilon} = \dfrac{t}{RC}$, which gives the solution below. The more charge already on the capacitor, the more it pushes back, so the charging slows down as it goes.

$$q = C\varepsilon\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right), \qquad I = \frac{dq}{dt} = \frac{\varepsilon}{R}e^{-t/RC}, \qquad V_C = \varepsilon\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right).$$
        After one time constant $\tau = RC$ the charge is 63% of its final value; after $5\tau$ it is over 99%.

The time constant sets the pace and nothing else: double $R$ or double $C$ and every stage of the charging takes twice as long, but the curves keep the same shape. Circuits use this to measure out time, from the blink rate of a flashing light to the delay before a camera flash is ready again.

blocks.html: Disconnect the battery from a charged capacitor and connect the capacitor across a resistor instead. Charge flows from one plate, through the resistor, to the other, and the capacitor empties. The equation is even simpler than charging, and its solution has a striking property: a fixed "half-life".

Around the loop the capacitor's voltage drives the current through the resistor: $\dfrac{q}{C} = IR$. The current drains the charge, $I = -\dfrac{dq}{dt}$, so
        $$\frac{dq}{dt} = -\frac{q}{RC}.$$
        The charge drains at a rate proportional to how much is left. Whenever "rate is proportional to amount", the solution is an exponential, $q = Q_0e^{-t/RC}$, the same law as radioactive decay.

$$q = Q_0e^{-t/RC}, \qquad V = V_0e^{-t/RC}, \qquad I = \frac{V_0}{R}e^{-t/RC}.$$
        The charge halves every $t_{1/2} = RC\ln 2 \approx 0.693\,RC$, however much there is. All of the stored energy, $\tfrac{1}{2}CV_0^2$, ends up as heat in the resistor.

"A capacitor with more charge takes longer to lose half of it." More charge means a higher voltage, which drives a bigger current, so it drains faster in exact proportion. blocks.html: In Physics 2 the magnetic force had a size, $qvB\sin\theta$, and a direction from the right-hand rule. The cross product packs both into one operation, and adding the electric force gives the complete force on a charge in any fields.

The Lorentz force: $$\vec{F} = q\left(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B}\right),$$ $$\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = \left(v_yB_z - v_zB_y,\ \ v_zB_x - v_xB_z,\ \ v_xB_y - v_yB_x\right).$$ For a negative charge, $q < 0$ reverses the force.

A cross product has exactly the properties the magnetic force has: its size is $vB\sin\theta$ (zero when $\vec{v}$ runs along $\vec{B}$, largest when they are perpendicular), and it points perpendicular to both $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$. Because the magnetic part is always perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, it does no work: $\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = 0$. A magnetic field can bend a charge's path but never speed it up or slow it down.

blocks.html: A Lorentz force with both an electric and a magnetic part can cancel itself. Arrange $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ at right angles, and for one particular speed the two pushes are equal and opposite. That is the heart of two classic instruments: the velocity selector and the mass spectrometer, which goes on to bend the selected ions into circles.

Velocity selector: with $\vec{E}\perp\vec{B}$, only charges with $$v = \frac{E}{B}$$ pass straight through, whatever their charge or mass.
Mass spectrometer: those charges then enter a field $B'$ alone and circle with radius $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB'}$, so $\dfrac{m}{q} = \dfrac{rB'}{v}$.

Straight through means no net force (Newton's first law): $qE = qvB$. The charge cancels from both sides, and the mass never appears, because nothing is accelerating. A faster particle feels a bigger magnetic force and curves one way; a slower one is pulled the other way by the electric force. Only $v = E/B$ survives the slit at the end. After the selector, every ion has the same speed, so the radius of its circle depends only on $m/q$.

blocks.html: Run a current across a magnetic field and the moving charges inside the conductor feel a sideways Lorentz force. They drift toward one edge, and charge piles up there until it pushes back. The small voltage that appears across the conductor is the Hall voltage. It does something remarkable: it tells you the sign of the moving charges, and how many there are. It connects directly to the drift velocity you already know.

For a strip of thickness $t$ (measured along $\vec{B}$) carrying current $I$: $$V_H = \frac{IB}{nqt}.$$ Positive and negative carriers are pushed to the same edge, so the sign of $V_H$ reveals the sign of the carriers.

The sideways magnetic force on each carrier is $qv_dB$. Charge builds up on the edge until its electric field $E_H$ pushes back just as hard: $qE_H = qv_dB$, so $E_H = v_dB$. Across a strip of width $w$, $V_H = E_Hw = v_dBw$. With $v_d = I/(nqwt)$ the width cancels: $V_H = IB/(nqt)$.
Why the same edge? Electrons drifting left feel $(-e)(-v\hat{\imath})\times\vec{B}$, which is the same as a positive charge drifting right. What differs is the sign of the charge that piles up, and so the sign of the voltage.

blocks.q: Current flows along $+x$ in a strip, $\vec{B}$ points along $+z$, and the $-y$ edge is at the higher potential. What are the carriers?
steps: Either kind of carrier is pushed toward $-y$ ($q\,\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ points along $-y$ for both).
The $-y$ edge is higher, so the charge piled up there is positive: the carriers are positive. (In a p-type semiconductor the carriers act as positive "holes".)

blocks.html: "The moving charges are always positive." Conventional current is drawn as if positive charges move, which works for circuits but hides who is really moving. In copper the carriers are electrons; in some semiconductors they behave as positive holes. Only the Hall voltage can tell the difference, because both kinds pile up on the same edge with opposite charges. Check: work out the force on both possibilities before deciding which edge is higher.

blocks.html: A current is a crowd of moving charges, so a wire in a magnetic field feels the sum of all their Lorentz forces. In Physics 2 that sum was $ILB\sin\theta$ for a straight wire in a uniform field. For bent wires and changing fields, add it up piece by piece.

$$d\vec{F} = I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\vec{B}, \qquad \vec{F} = I\int d\vec{\ell}\times\vec{B}.$$ In a uniform field this becomes $\vec{F} = I\,\vec{L}\times\vec{B}$, where $\vec{L}$ is the straight-line displacement from the wire's start to its end, whatever its shape. A closed loop in a uniform field feels no net force.

A piece of wire of length $d\ell$ holds charge $dq$ moving at $\vec{v}$, and $dq\,\vec{v} = I\,d\vec{\ell}$ (charge per time times distance). So each piece feels $dq\,\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\vec{B}$. If $\vec{B}$ is the same everywhere, $I$ and $\vec{B}$ come out of the integral, leaving $\int d\vec{\ell}$: the sum of all the little steps along the wire, which is just the displacement from start to finish. Around a closed loop you end where you started, so that sum is zero.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field. Change the angle: the force is $ILB\sin\theta$, perpendicular to both the wire and the field.

blocks.title: A half circle
blocks.q: A wire bent into a half circle of radius $10\ \text{cm}$ carries $4.0\ \text{A}$ in a uniform $0.50\ \text{T}$ field perpendicular to its plane. Find the force.
steps: The displacement from one end to the other is a diameter, $2R = 0.20\ \text{m}$, perpendicular to $\vec{B}$.
Check by integrating: each piece feels $IBR\,d\phi$ pointing outward; the parts along the diameter cancel, and the rest add to $\int_0^\pi IBR\sin\phi\,d\phi = 2IBR$.

blocks.title: Any path, same answer
blocks.q: A wire carrying $3.0\ \text{A}$ wanders from $(0, 0)$ to $(0.30, 0.40)\ \text{m}$ in a uniform $0.20\ \text{T}$ field along $+z$. Find the size of the force.
steps: Only the displacement counts: $|\vec{L}| = \sqrt{0.30^2 + 0.40^2} = 0.50\ \text{m}$, perpendicular to $\vec{B}$.

blocks.title: A field that changes along the wire
blocks.q: A long wire carries $20\ \text{A}$. A rod carrying $5.0\ \text{A}$ lies perpendicular to it, from $2.0$ to $10\ \text{cm}$ away. Find the force on the rod.
steps: Now $\vec{B}$ is not uniform: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r}$, perpendicular to the rod all along it.

blocks.html: "A current loop in a uniform field is pushed sideways." Each side does feel a force, but the forces on opposite sides are equal and opposite, and around the whole loop they add to zero, since $\oint d\vec{\ell} = 0$. What the loop can feel is a torque, which turns it without moving it, and that is how motors work. A loop is pushed as a whole only when the field is stronger on one side than the other.

blocks.html: A current loop in a uniform field feels no net force, but the forces on opposite sides need not act along the same line. Two equal, opposite, offset forces make a twist: a torque. That twist drives every electric motor and the needle of every old-style meter.

A flat loop of $N$ turns, current $I$ and area $A$ has a magnetic moment $\vec{\mu} = NIA\,\hat{n}$, along its normal by the right-hand rule (fingers along the current, thumb along $\hat{n}$). In a field: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}, \qquad \tau = \mu B\sin\theta, \qquad U = -\vec{\mu}\cdot\vec{B},$$ with $\theta$ the angle between $\vec{\mu}$ (the normal) and $\vec{B}$.

Take a rectangular loop with sides $a$ and $b$. The two sides of length $a$ cut across the field and feel forces $IaB$ in opposite directions. Each acts a distance $\tfrac{b}{2}$ from the axis, with lever arm $\tfrac{b}{2}\sin\theta$. Together: $\tau = 2(IaB)\left(\tfrac{b}{2}\sin\theta\right) = I(ab)B\sin\theta = IAB\sin\theta$. The forces on the other two sides point along the axis and only stretch the loop. Since only the area appears, the result holds for any flat loop.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: A loop in a motor. The torque is largest when the field lies in the plane of the loop and zero when the field passes straight through it; a commutator reverses the current each half turn so the loop keeps turning.

blocks.title: Moment and greatest torque
blocks.q: A 50-turn square coil $4.0\ \text{cm}$ on a side carries $2.0\ \text{A}$ in a $0.30\ \text{T}$ field. Find $\mu$ and the largest torque.

blocks.title: An angle given to the plane
blocks.q: The same coil is turned so its plane makes $30^\circ$ with the field. Find the torque.
steps: The normal is $90^\circ$ from the plane, so $\theta = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$.

blocks.title: Turning it over
blocks.q: How much work does it take to turn the coil from $\theta = 0$ (moment along the field) to $\theta = 180^\circ$?
steps: $U = -\mu B\cos\theta$ goes from $-\mu B$ to $+\mu B$.

blocks.html: "The torque is greatest when the field passes straight through the loop." That is where the flux is greatest, but the torque is zero there: the forces on opposite sides then pull straight outward along one line, with no lever arm. Check with $\tau = \mu B\sin\theta$: field straight through means $\theta = 0$ and $\sin\theta = 0$. Always measure $\theta$ from the normal, not from the plane.

blocks.html: So far we have taken the fields of wires and solenoids from Physics 2 as given. Where do they come from? Every small piece of current makes its own small field, and the total is the sum, just as charge pieces added up to an electric field. The rule for one piece is the Biot–Savart law, the magnetic partner of Coulomb's law.

A piece of wire $d\vec{\ell}$ carrying current $I$ makes, at a point a distance $r$ away in the direction $\hat{r}$,
        $$d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}, \qquad dB = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{I\,d\ell\,\sin\theta}{r^2},$$
        with $\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7}\ \text{T·m/A}$ and $\theta$ the angle between $d\vec{\ell}$ and $\hat{r}$.

Compare with a charge piece's field, $k\,dq/r^2$: both fall off as $1/r^2$ and grow with the source. The difference is direction. A current piece has a direction of its own, $d\vec{\ell}$, and its field circles around it, perpendicular to both $d\vec{\ell}$ and $\hat{r}$, which the cross product captures. Points straight ahead of or behind a current piece ($\theta = 0$ or $180^\circ$) get no field from it at all.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: Biot–Savart, piece by piece: each element of the wire adds a small $d\vec{B}$ at P, perpendicular to both the element and the line to P. Elements straight in line with P add nothing.

blocks.title: One small piece
blocks.q: A $1.0\ \text{mm}$ piece of wire carries $10\ \text{A}$. Find its field at a point $5.0\ \text{cm}$ away, along a line at $30^\circ$ to the current.

blocks.title: A straight segment
blocks.q: A straight segment $10\ \text{cm}$ long carries $10\ \text{A}$. Find the field $5.0\ \text{cm}$ from its midpoint on the perpendicular bisector. Then let the wire become infinitely long.
steps: A piece at $x$ is $r = \sqrt{x^2 + d^2}$ away, with $\sin\theta = d/r$, and every piece's field points the same way (around the wire), so the sizes add: $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\int_{-a}^{a}\frac{d\,dx}{(x^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}\cdot\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2 + d^2}}$$
For an endless wire, $a \to \infty$ and the last fraction becomes 1: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$, the Physics 2 formula, now derived.

blocks.title: The center of a square loop
blocks.q: A square loop with $10\ \text{cm}$ sides carries $10\ \text{A}$. Find the field at its center.
steps: Each side is a segment with $a = d = s/2$, so each gives $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(s/2)}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, and all four point the same way at the center.

blocks.html: Dropping the $\sin\theta$. Without it, every piece of a straight wire, even pieces lined up with the point, would contribute fully, and the field at a point on the wire's own line would come out large instead of zero. The cross product says a current makes no field straight ahead of itself. Check: for a point on the extension of a straight segment, every $\theta$ is $0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$, and $B$ must be $0$.

blocks.html: With Biot–Savart we can find the field of a current loop, the building block of solenoids, electromagnets and, on a tiny scale, magnetic atoms. As with the charged ring, symmetry does most of the work.

At the center: every piece $d\ell$ is the same distance $R$ away and at right angles to the line to the center, and every piece's field points the same way (along the axis). So $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}\oint d\ell = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$. An arc covering angle $\phi$ gives the same fraction of that: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I\phi}{4\pi R}$.
On the axis: each piece is $\sqrt{z^2 + R^2}$ away; the sideways parts cancel around the loop, and the parts along the axis carry a factor $R/\sqrt{z^2 + R^2}$.

Center of a loop: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$ (times $N$ for $N$ turns). Center of an arc of angle $\phi$ (radians): $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I\phi}{4\pi R}$. On the axis:
        $$B = \frac{\mu_0 IR^2}{2(z^2 + R^2)^{3/2}},$$
        which far away falls as $1/z^3$, the field of a magnetic dipole.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: The field of a current loop: lines through the middle, curling back around the wire, like the field of a short bar magnet.

blocks.title: A flat coil
blocks.q: A flat coil of 20 turns with radius $5.0\ \text{cm}$ carries $2.0\ \text{A}$. Find $B$ at its center.
steps: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R} = \dfrac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7})(20)(2.0)}{2(0.050)} = 5.03 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{T}$, about $503\ \mu\text{T}$, ten times Earth's field.

blocks.title: A quarter circle
blocks.q: A quarter-circle arc of radius $4.0\ \text{cm}$ carries $5.0\ \text{A}$. Find its field at the center.
steps: That is one quarter of a full loop's $\mu_0 I/(2R)$, as it should be.

blocks.title: Moving out along the axis
blocks.q: How strong is a loop's field on its axis at $z = 2R$, compared with the center?
steps: Less than a tenth, two radii out. Far away, $B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0 IR^2}{2z^3}$.

blocks.html: Far from a loop, its field has the same shape as a bar magnet's, and both are called magnetic dipoles. Earth's field far out in space looks much like this. Close to a pair of coils the field can be shaped instead: two identical coils, one radius apart and carrying the same current, make a field that is very nearly uniform in the space between them, a common way to make a known field in a lab.

Using the long-straight-wire formula at the center of a loop. $\mu_0 I/(2\pi R)$ is the field a distance $R$ from a straight wire, a different shape. At the center of a loop, all the wire is the same distance away and bent around the point, so its contributions add more effectively, giving $\mu_0 I/(2R)$, larger by a factor of $\pi$. Check: which shape is the wire? A loop's formula has no $\pi$ in it.

blocks.html: Biot–Savart always works but often means a hard integral. For electric fields, Gauss's law gave a shortcut when the charge had symmetry. Magnetism has its own shortcut, built not on flux through a closed surface but on the field around a closed path.

Ampère's law: around any closed path, $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}},$$ where $I_{\text{enc}}$ is the net current through any surface bounded by the path. Sign: curl the fingers of your right hand along the path; current along your thumb counts as positive. Currents outside the path do not count.

Start with one long wire and a circle around it. The field is $\mu_0 I/(2\pi r)$ and points along the circle, so $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\cdot 2\pi r = \mu_0 I$: the radius cancels. For any path, $\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ around a wire is $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}\,d\varphi$, where $d\varphi$ is the angle the step sweeps out as seen from the wire. A path that goes around the wire sweeps a full $2\pi$; a path that does not enclose it sweeps out and back, for a total angle of zero. Fields add, so each enclosed current adds its own $\mu_0 I$.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: Ampère's law: drag the dashed path. $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ changes only when a wire crosses the path, never when an outside wire moves.

blocks.title: Counting currents
blocks.q: A path circles counterclockwise (seen from above) around a wire carrying $5.0\ \text{A}$ up (out of the page) and one carrying $2.0\ \text{A}$ down. A third wire, outside the path, carries $3.0\ \text{A}$. Find $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$.
steps: Counterclockwise: out of the page is positive. $I_{\text{enc}} = 5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0\ \text{A}$; the outside wire does not count.

blocks.title: The field of a long wire, from symmetry
blocks.q: Use Ampère's law to find $B$ at $2.0\ \text{cm}$ from a long wire carrying $10\ \text{A}$.
steps: By symmetry $\vec{B}$ circles the wire with the same size all around a circle of radius $r$, and points along it. So $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = B(2\pi r)$.

blocks.title: Going the other way around
blocks.q: What is $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$ for the first path if you go around it clockwise instead?
steps: Reversing the path reverses every $d\vec{\ell}$, so the integral changes sign: $-3.77 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{T·m}$.
The right-hand rule agrees: clockwise makes into-the-page positive, so $I_{\text{enc}} = 2.0 - 5.0 = -3.0\ \text{A}$.

blocks.html: Counting currents outside the path. An outside wire does change $\vec{B}$ at every point of the path, so it feels as if it should count. But going around, its field helps on the near side and opposes on the far side, and those parts cancel exactly in the integral. Check: only currents that pierce a surface spanning the path go into $I_{\text{enc}}$.

Like Gauss's law, Ampère's law is always true, but it hands you $B$ only when symmetry makes $\vec{B}$ constant and along the path on the parts that matter. It also needs one correction when currents change in time: the displacement current.

blocks.html: Ampère's law finds fields in one line when you can choose a path where $\vec{B}$ is constant and runs along the path (or is zero). Three shapes allow this: a long straight wire (inside and out), a long solenoid, and a toroid.

Inside a wire of radius $R$ with current spread evenly: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2}$; outside, $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.
Long solenoid with $n$ turns per meter: $B = \mu_0 nI$ inside, nearly zero outside.
Toroid of $N$ turns, inside the windings: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2\pi r}$.

Wire: a circle of radius $r$ inside the wire encloses the fraction $r^2/R^2$ of the current, so $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I r^2/R^2$.
Solenoid: use a rectangle with one long side of length $\ell$ inside, along the axis, and the other outside. Outside the field is negligible, and on the short sides $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to the path. Only the inside side counts: $B\ell = \mu_0(n\ell)I$.
Toroid: a circle of radius $r$ inside the doughnut links all $N$ turns: $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 NI$. Unlike a solenoid's, the field is weaker toward the outer edge.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: A solenoid: a strong, nearly uniform field inside, a weak field outside. Ampère's law with a rectangular path gives $B = \mu_0 nI$.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: A toroid: the field stays inside the doughnut and falls off as $1/r$ across it.

blocks.html: Fusion machines such as tokamaks and stellarators hold hot plasma in a toroid's field. Because that field is weaker toward the outside of the doughnut, a field that only runs around the ring cannot hold the plasma: the charged particles drift, and the plasma is pushed outward. So these machines give the field lines a twist, winding them into helices. Explore twisted magnetic bottles in Magnetic Bottles for Fusion in the Science Lab.

blocks.title: Inside a thick wire
blocks.q: A wire of radius $2.0\ \text{mm}$ carries $10\ \text{A}$ spread evenly. Find $B$ at $1.0\ \text{mm}$ from the axis and at the surface.
steps: At the surface, $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} = 1.00\ \text{mT}$: the field grows linearly from zero at the axis to its peak at the surface, then falls as $1/r$.

blocks.title: A solenoid
blocks.q: A solenoid $25\ \text{cm}$ long has 500 turns and carries $2.0\ \text{A}$. Find $B$ inside.

blocks.title: A toroid
blocks.q: A toroid of 1000 turns carries $1.0\ \text{A}$. Its windings run from $8.0$ to $12\ \text{cm}$ from the center. Find $B$ at the inner and outer edges of the windings.

blocks.html: "The magnetic field inside a current-carrying wire is zero, like the electric field inside a charged conductor." That electric rule holds only when no charge is moving. In a wire carrying current, the current itself is inside, and an Ampère circle inside the wire encloses part of it. Check with the first example: halfway out, $B$ is half the surface value, not zero. Only on the axis is $B = 0$.
