blocks.html: Magnetic flux, $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$, counts how much field passes through a loop. Faraday's law, next, says that what matters for induction is how fast the flux changes. So before using it, we need to see every way flux can change, and how to find it when the field is not uniform.

$$\Phi_B = \int \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}\qquad(\text{webers: } 1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T·m}^2)$$
        For a uniform field and a flat loop, $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$ with $\theta$ from the normal. The flux changes when $B$ changes, when the area changes, or when the angle changes.

The dot product picks out the part of $\vec{B}$ that crosses the surface, exactly as for electric flux. When $\vec{B}$ varies across the loop, the loop must be cut into strips where it is nearly constant, and the strips added with an integral. Each of the three factors can change in time: a magnet moving closer changes $B$, a sliding rod changes $A$, and a spinning coil changes $\theta$, even in a perfectly steady field.

blocks.name: ph-induction
blocks.cap: Flux through a tilted loop in a uniform field. Turn the loop: the flux is largest when the field goes straight through and zero when the loop is edge-on.

blocks.title: A tilted loop
blocks.q: A square loop $10\ \text{cm}$ on a side sits in a uniform $0.40\ \text{T}$ field, with its normal at $60^\circ$ to the field. Find the flux.

blocks.title: Turning in a steady field
blocks.q: The same loop is turned until its normal is at $90^\circ$ to the field. How much did the flux change?

blocks.title: Beside a long wire
blocks.q: A long wire carries $20\ \text{A}$. A rectangular loop in the same plane has sides of $20\ \text{cm}$ parallel to the wire, at $2.0$ and $10\ \text{cm}$ from it. Find the flux.
steps: The field $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ is stronger near the wire, so use strips parallel to the wire, of area $(0.20)\,dr$, each with one value of $B$.

blocks.html: "A steady field cannot change the flux." It can, if the loop turns: $\cos\theta$ changes even though $B$ does not. That is exactly how a generator works, spinning coils in the steady field of a magnet. Check by listing all three factors in $BA\cos\theta$ and asking which of them is changing.

blocks.html: You know Faraday's law as "a changing flux makes an emf", with Lenz's law giving the direction. With flux as a function of time and the derivative, we can find the emf at any instant, not just an average over an interval.

$$\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}.$$ The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current makes a field that opposes the change. For $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, the product and chain rules give one term for each thing that changes.

Faraday found that the emf depends on how fast the flux changes, not on how big it is. "How fast, at this instant" is a derivative. Dividing a change by a time interval, $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$, only gives the average emf over that interval; letting the interval shrink to zero gives the emf at one moment. The sign is fixed by energy: if the induced current reinforced the change, it would feed itself without limit.

blocks.name: ph-induction
blocks.cap: A coil in a field that ramps up, holds steady, then ramps down. The emf graph follows the slope of the flux graph: zero while the flux is steady, however large it is.

blocks.title: A field that speeds up
blocks.q: A 50-turn coil of area $0.010\ \text{m}^2$ sits in a perpendicular field $B = 0.020t^2 + 0.10t$ (tesla, seconds). Find the emf at $t = 2.0\ \text{s}$.

blocks.title: A growing loop
blocks.q: A circular loop in a steady $0.50\ \text{T}$ field (perpendicular to it) grows: its radius is $10\ \text{cm}$ and increasing at $2.0\ \text{cm/s}$. Find the emf.
steps: $\Phi = B\pi r^2$, so $\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = B\cdot 2\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt}$ by the chain rule.

blocks.title: Average or instant?
blocks.q: A field through a loop rises from $0$ to $0.50\ \text{T}$ in $10\ \text{s}$, all of it in the last second. Compare the average emf with the emf during that last second.
steps: For the first $9\ \text{s}$ nothing changes, so the emf is zero. In the last second the flux changes ten times faster than the average rate, so the emf is ten times the average.
blocks.a: zero, then ten times the average

blocks.html: Using an average $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$ over a long time when the question asks for the emf at one instant. Unless the flux changes at a steady rate, the average hides what happens at any particular moment. Write $\Phi(t)$, differentiate it, and put in the time you want. Check: if $\Phi(t)$ is not a straight line in time, the emf cannot be constant.

blocks.html: Spin a coil in a steady magnetic field and its flux rises and falls over and over. Faraday's law turns that into an emf that swings back and forth: alternating current. Almost all of the world's electricity comes from machines built on this idea.

A coil of $N$ turns, each of area $A$, turning at angular speed $\omega$ in a field $B$:
        $$\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t, \qquad \varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t,$$
        with peak emf $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$ and $\omega = 2\pi f$.

The angle between the coil's normal and the field grows steadily, $\theta = \omega t$, so the flux through each turn is $BA\cos\omega t$. Differentiating, $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d}{dt}(NBA\cos\omega t) = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$. The emf is largest when $\sin\omega t = \pm 1$, which is when $\cos\omega t = 0$: the coil is edge-on to the field and the flux is zero, but changing fastest. Spinning faster raises both the frequency and the peak emf.

blocks.name: ph-induction
blocks.cap: A generator: the flux (top graph) and the emf (bottom graph) are a quarter cycle apart. The emf peaks when the flux passes through zero.

blocks.title: Peak emf
blocks.q: A 100-turn coil of area $0.020\ \text{m}^2$ spins at $60\ \text{Hz}$ in a $0.25\ \text{T}$ field. Find the peak emf.

blocks.title: At a given angle
blocks.q: What is that generator's emf when the coil's normal is $30^\circ$ from the field?
steps: At $0^\circ$ (field straight through) it would be zero; at $90^\circ$ (edge-on), the full $188\ \text{V}$.

blocks.title: From rpm
blocks.q: A coil turning at 1800 revolutions per minute: what is $\omega$?

blocks.html: "The emf is largest when the most field passes through the coil." At that moment the flux is at its peak, so for an instant it is not changing, and the emf is zero. Faraday's law follows the slope of $\Phi(t)$, not its height. Check with the graphs: the emf curve crosses zero exactly where the flux curve is at a peak.

A motor is a generator run backward, and it is a generator at the same time: its spinning coil makes an emf that opposes the supply, called the back emf. That is why a motor draws its largest current when it is just starting, before it spins up.

blocks.html: When Faraday's law drives a current around a loop, something must push the charges along the wire. A magnetic force needs moving charges, but here the charges may start at rest. The push is an electric field, made not by charges but by the changing magnetic field itself. It exists whether or not a wire is there to feel it.

$$\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$$
        around any closed path, in matter or in empty space. Inside a long solenoid of radius $R$ whose field changes, the induced field circles the axis with $E = \dfrac{r}{2}\dfrac{dB}{dt}$ ($r < R$) and $E = \dfrac{R^2}{2r}\dfrac{dB}{dt}$ ($r > R$).

The emf of a loop is the work per unit charge done around it, $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$. Faraday's law says this equals $-d\Phi_B/dt$. Unlike the field of still charges, this field curls around: its integral around a closed loop is not zero, so it has no potential (you cannot speak of the voltage between two points). Around a solenoid, symmetry says the field lines are circles, so $\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = E(2\pi r)$, which equals the rate of change of the flux inside the circle. This is the method of Ampère's law, used for $\vec{E}$.

$E = \dfrac{R^2}{2r}\dfrac{dB}{dt} = \dfrac{(0.050)^2(0.20)}{2(0.10)} = 2.50\ \text{mV/m}$, in a place where the magnetic field itself is nearly zero.

blocks.html: "The induced field needs a wire to exist." The wire only provides free charges for the field to push, so that a current flows. The field itself is made by the changing magnetic field, in empty space as well as in metal. Electrons circling in a vacuum tube can be sped up this way; a machine called the betatron did exactly that. Check: Faraday's law mentions a closed path, not a conductor.

blocks.html: A rod sliding on rails in a magnetic field makes a motional emf $BLv$ and drives a current. That current sits in the field, so it feels a force. Lenz's law decides which way, and the answer makes the rod behave exactly like an object moving through a fluid with linear drag.

A rod of length $L$ moving at $v$ on rails closed by a resistance $R$ feels a magnetic force
        $$F = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R}$$
        against its motion. Left to coast, $v = v_0e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau = \dfrac{mR}{B^2L^2}$, and it travels a total distance $v_0\tau$. Falling on vertical rails, it reaches a terminal speed $v_T = \dfrac{mgR}{B^2L^2}$.

Follow the chain: speed makes emf, $\varepsilon = BLv$; emf drives current, $I = BLv/R$; current in a field feels force, $F = ILB = B^2L^2v/R$. The force is proportional to the speed, like drag $F = -bv$ with $b = B^2L^2/R$. Newton's law $m\,dv/dt = -bv$ then gives exponential decay. Energy check: the rod's kinetic energy turns into heat in the resistor, $I^2R$, so the force must oppose the motion.

Heating: $P = mgv_T = (0.050)(9.8)(1.96) = 0.960\ \text{W}$. All the gravitational energy lost each second becomes heat.

blocks.html: "The induced current pushes the rod along." If it did, the rod would speed up, inducing more current and more push, gaining energy from nowhere. Lenz's law (and energy conservation) says the force opposes the motion. Check the direction with the right-hand rule: the force $I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}$ on the induced current always points against $\vec{v}$. This is how eddy-current brakes on some trains and amusement rides slow them smoothly without touching anything.

blocks.html: A coil's own current makes a magnetic field through the coil itself. Change the current and that flux changes, so the coil induces an emf in itself. A coil built to make use of this is an inductor, and the strength of the effect is its self-inductance.

$$\varepsilon = -L\frac{dI}{dt}, \qquad L = \frac{N\Phi_B}{I}.$$
        Unit: the henry, $1\ \text{H} = 1\ \text{V·s/A}$. For a long solenoid of $N$ turns, length $\ell$ and cross-section $A$, $L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{\ell}$.

The flux a coil makes through itself is proportional to its current, so $N\Phi = LI$ for some constant $L$ fixed by the coil's shape. Faraday's law then gives $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$. For a solenoid, $B = \mu_0(N/\ell)I$, so $N\Phi = N\cdot\mu_0\dfrac{N}{\ell}I\cdot A$ and $L = \mu_0N^2A/\ell$. The $N^2$ appears because more turns make a stronger field and give that field more turns to thread. The minus sign means the emf fights the change: an inductor makes current sluggish, like mass makes motion sluggish.

blocks.html: Every circuit has some inductance, since every current makes a field around its own wire, but coils concentrate it. Winding the coil on an iron core multiplies $L$ by hundreds or thousands, because the iron's atoms line up with the coil's field and add their own. That is why transformers, motors and the chokes in power supplies are built around iron.

"An inductor opposes current." It opposes changes in current. A steady current, however large, has $dI/dt = 0$ and meets no back emf at all; the inductor then acts like a plain wire. Check with $\varepsilon = -L\,dI/dt$: the formula contains the rate of change, not the current itself.

blocks.html: Two coils near each other share flux. A changing current in one changes the flux through the other, and Faraday's law induces an emf there, with no wire between them. This is inductance between two coils instead of within one, and it is how transformers, wireless chargers and many sensors work.

$$M = \frac{N_2\Phi_{21}}{I_1}, \qquad \varepsilon_2 = -M\frac{dI_1}{dt}.$$
        In an ideal transformer every turn of both coils shares the same changing flux, so
        $$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}, \qquad I_sV_s = I_pV_p.$$

The flux coil 1 sends through coil 2 is proportional to $I_1$; the constant of proportionality, per turn of coil 2, is $M$. In a transformer an iron core guides nearly all the flux of the primary through the secondary, so each turn of either coil has the same emf, $-d\Phi/dt$. More turns add more emf: voltage per turn is the same on both sides. An ideal transformer stores and wastes no energy, so the power in equals the power out, and raising the voltage must lower the current.

steps: Inside the solenoid, $B = \mu_0\dfrac{N_1}{\ell}I_1$, and each turn of the outer coil holds flux $BA$ (outside the solenoid the field is negligible).

blocks.html: "A transformer that raises the voltage also raises the power." A transformer is not an energy source. Stepping the voltage up 20 times steps the current down 20 times, so $IV$ stays the same (a real transformer loses a little to heat). Check: compute $I_pV_p$ and $I_sV_s$; for an ideal transformer they must match. Also note that a transformer needs a changing current: steady DC makes no changing flux and no output.

blocks.html: Put an inductor in series with a resistor and a battery. Because the inductor fights every change in current, the current cannot jump when the switch closes; it grows smoothly, in a curve you have seen before in charging a capacitor.

Loop rule, with the inductor's back emf: $\varepsilon - IR - L\dfrac{dI}{dt} = 0$, so
        $$\frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{\varepsilon - IR}{L} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dI}{\varepsilon/R - I} = \frac{R}{L}\,dt.$$
        Integrating from $I = 0$ at $t = 0$ gives $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R}\left(1 - e^{-Rt/L}\right)$. At first $I = 0$, so the whole battery voltage sits across the inductor: the current starts rising at the rate $\varepsilon/L$. As $I$ grows, more voltage goes to the resistor and the rise slows.

$$I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \qquad V_L = \varepsilon e^{-t/\tau}, \qquad \tau = \frac{L}{R}.$$
        If the battery is removed and the loop stays closed through a resistance $R$, the current dies away as $I = I_0e^{-t/\tau}$.

$I = 1.2e^{-1} = 0.441\ \text{A}$. The inductor keeps the current flowing for a while after the battery is gone.

blocks.html: "The current jumps to $\varepsilon/R$ the instant the switch closes." A sudden jump would need an infinite $dI/dt$, and so an infinite back emf. Instead the inductor takes the whole battery voltage at the start and the current begins at zero. Check with the loop rule at $t = 0$: $I = 0$, so $L\,dI/dt = \varepsilon$. (A capacitor is the opposite: its current jumps at once and its voltage builds slowly.)

blocks.html: Building up a current in an inductor takes work, because the back emf pushes against the current the whole time. That work is not lost: it is stored, and it comes back out when the current falls. Just as a capacitor's energy lives in its electric field, an inductor's lives in its magnetic field.

An inductor carrying current $I$ stores $U = \tfrac{1}{2}LI^2$. A magnetic field stores energy with density
        $$u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\quad(\text{J/m}^3).$$

While the current rises, the source must push charge against the back emf $L\,dI/dt$. The power it supplies to the inductor is $L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\,I$, so the work to go from $0$ to $I$ is $$W = \int_0^I LI'\,dI' = \tfrac{1}{2}LI^2.$$ For a long solenoid, $L = \mu_0N^2A/\ell$ and $B = \mu_0NI/\ell$, so $\tfrac{1}{2}LI^2 = \dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0}(A\ell)$: the energy density $B^2/(2\mu_0)$ times the volume holding the field.

blocks.html: The stored energy is also why the current in an RL circuit keeps flowing for a while after the battery is removed: the field's $\tfrac{1}{2}LI^2$ drives the current until the resistor has turned all of it into heat. In an LC circuit, the same energy flows into a capacitor instead, and comes back.

Mixing the inductor and capacitor formulas, writing $\tfrac{1}{2}LV^2$ or $\tfrac{1}{2}CI^2$. Each device's energy depends on what builds its field: current for an inductor ($\tfrac{1}{2}LI^2$), voltage, that is charge, for a capacitor ($\tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$). Check with units: H·A² = (V·s/A)·A² = V·A·s = J, while H·V² is not a joule.

blocks.html: Connect a charged capacitor to an inductor, with no resistor and no battery. The capacitor starts to discharge, but the inductor will not let the current stop: when the capacitor is empty, the current keeps going and charges it the other way. Energy sloshes back and forth between the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field, exactly the way it moves between a spring and a mass.

Around the loop, the capacitor's voltage equals the inductor's emf: $\dfrac{q}{C} = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$, with $I = dq/dt$. So $$L\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{q}{C} = 0,$$ the equation of simple harmonic motion with $q$ in place of $x$. Its solution is $q = Q_0\cos\omega t$ with $\omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{LC}$.

$$\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad q = Q_0\cos\omega t, \qquad I = -Q_0\omega\sin\omega t.$$
        The total energy $\dfrac{q^2}{2C} + \tfrac{1}{2}LI^2 = \dfrac{Q_0^2}{2C}$ stays constant. The current is largest, $Q_0\omega$, when the capacitor is empty.

When the capacitor is fully charged, all the energy is in its electric field and the current is momentarily zero, like a pendulum at the end of its swing. The current peaks a quarter cycle later, when the capacitor is empty and all the energy is in the inductor. Check: $q = Q_0\cos\omega t$ and $I = -Q_0\omega\sin\omega t$ are never largest at the same time.

blocks.html: Real circuits have resistance, so LC oscillations do not last forever: each cycle the resistor turns a little of the energy into heat. The result is a damped oscillation, the electrical twin of a damped spring.

Add the resistor's voltage to the loop rule: $L\ddot{q} + R\dot{q} + \dfrac{q}{C} = 0$. Compare $m\ddot{x} + b\dot{x} + kx = 0$: the resistance plays the role of the drag constant. So everything you know about damped springs carries over. For small $R$ the charge still oscillates, but inside a shrinking envelope:
        $$q = Q_0e^{-Rt/2L}\cos(\omega' t + \phi), \qquad \omega' = \sqrt{\frac{1}{LC} - \left(\frac{R}{2L}\right)^2}.$$

Underdamped ($R < 2\sqrt{L/C}$): oscillation with amplitude falling as $e^{-Rt/2L}$ and energy as $e^{-Rt/L}$. Critically damped at $R = 2\sqrt{L/C}$; overdamped above it, with no oscillation at all. Light damping barely changes the frequency.

blocks.html: "Adding resistance changes the frequency a lot." For light damping the correction $(R/2L)^2$ is tiny next to $1/(LC)$: in the first example it shifts the frequency by about half a percent. What you notice is the amplitude dying away. blocks.html: A generator makes an emf that swings back and forth as $\sin\omega t$, and that is what comes out of a wall outlet. A voltage that spends half its time negative raises a question: how do you describe its "size", and how much power does it deliver? The answer is the rms value, the number printed on every appliance.

$V = V_0\sin\omega t$. Its rms (root-mean-square) value is $$V_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}},$$ and likewise $I_{\text{rms}} = I_0/\sqrt{2}$. A resistor's average power is $\bar{P} = I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}} = V_{\text{rms}}^2/R$, the same as a steady voltage of $V_{\text{rms}}$ would give.

Power in a resistor is $V^2/R$, and $V^2 = V_0^2\sin^2\omega t$ is never negative, so the power is positive all the time even though $V$ averages to zero. Over a whole cycle, $\sin^2$ and $\cos^2$ average to the same value, and they add to 1 at every instant, so each averages to $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Then $\bar{P} = \dfrac{V_0^2}{2R} = \dfrac{(V_0/\sqrt{2})^2}{R}$. Squaring, averaging (mean) and taking the root is exactly how $V_{\text{rms}}$ is defined, which is where the name comes from.

$V_{\text{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt{3} \approx 0.577V_0$, a bit less than a sine wave's $0.707V_0$. The factor $1/\sqrt{2}$ belongs to sine waves only.

blocks.html: A resistor obeys $V = IR$ at every instant. A capacitor or an inductor in an AC circuit also limits the current, but in its own way: by an amount that depends on the frequency, and with its current out of step with its voltage. The "resistance" of each is called its reactance.

$$X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}, \qquad X_L = \omega L, \qquad I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{X}.$$ In a capacitor the current leads the voltage by $90^\circ$; in an inductor it lags by $90^\circ$. Neither uses any average power.

Capacitor: $q = CV$, so $I = C\dfrac{dV}{dt}$. With $V = V_0\sin\omega t$, $I = \omega CV_0\cos\omega t$: the peak current is $\omega CV_0 = V_0/X_C$. The cosine peaks a quarter cycle before the sine, so the current leads. At high frequency the capacitor is charged and discharged so quickly that it never fills up, so it passes current easily: $X_C$ falls.
Inductor: $V = L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$. With $I = I_0\sin\omega t$, $V = \omega LI_0\cos\omega t$: peak voltage $\omega LI_0 = X_LI_0$, and the voltage leads, so the current lags. The faster the current tries to change, the harder the inductor fights: $X_L$ rises with frequency.

steps: $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(0.050)(10 \times 10^{-6})}} = 225\ \text{Hz}$. This is the resonant frequency you will meet soon.

blocks.html: Because the two reactances move in opposite directions, capacitors and inductors sort signals by frequency. In a loudspeaker crossover, a capacitor in series with the small tweeter lets the high notes through and holds back the low ones, while an inductor in series with the large woofer does the reverse.

"A capacitor's reactance grows with frequency." It shrinks: $X_C = 1/(\omega C)$. At high frequency a capacitor behaves almost like a wire, and at zero frequency (steady DC) it blocks completely, once charged. It is the inductor whose reactance grows. Check with the extremes: DC through a capacitor is blocked ($X_C \to \infty$ as $\omega \to 0$); DC through an inductor flows freely ($X_L \to 0$).

blocks.html: Put a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor in series on an AC source. The same current flows through all three, but their voltages peak at different times, a quarter cycle apart. To add them you need a way to add oscillations that are out of step: phasors.

$$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \qquad \tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}, \qquad I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z},$$ where $\phi$ is the angle by which the source voltage leads the current. The impedance $Z$ plays the part of resistance for the whole circuit.

Picture each oscillating voltage as an arrow (a phasor) spinning at $\omega$, whose shadow on the vertical axis is the actual voltage. Take the current's arrow as the reference. $V_R = IR$ points along it; $V_L = IX_L$ points $90^\circ$ ahead; $V_C = IX_C$ points $90^\circ$ behind, so it is opposite to $V_L$. The source voltage is the vector sum: $V_L$ and $V_C$ partly cancel, leaving $I(X_L - X_C)$ at right angles to $IR$. Pythagoras gives $V = I\sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, and the angle of the sum is $\phi$.

blocks.name: ph-circuit
blocks.cap: A series RLC circuit with its phasors: $V_R$ along the current, $V_L$ and $V_C$ pointing opposite ways. Change the frequency and watch which one wins.

blocks.title: From reactances
blocks.q: $R = 30\ \Omega$, $X_L = 80\ \Omega$ and $X_C = 40\ \Omega$ in series. Find $Z$ and $\phi$.
steps: $\tan\phi = 40/30$, so $\phi = 53.1^\circ$: the voltage leads, since the inductor dominates.

blocks.title: A full circuit
blocks.q: $R = 40\ \Omega$, $L = 0.10\ \text{H}$ and $C = 50\ \mu\text{F}$ in series on $120\ \text{V}$ rms at $60\ \text{Hz}$. Find $Z$, the current and $\phi$.
steps: $\tan\phi = \dfrac{-15.4}{40}$, so $\phi = -21.0^\circ$: negative, the circuit is more capacitive and the voltage lags the current.

blocks.title: More voltage than the source
blocks.q: In the same circuit, find the rms voltages across the inductor and the capacitor.
steps: $V_C$ is larger than the source's $120\ \text{V}$! It is no contradiction: $V_L$ and $V_C$ are opposite in phase and mostly cancel, so the three voltages do not add as plain numbers.

blocks.html: Adding $R$, $X_L$ and $X_C$ as plain numbers. That treats three voltages that peak at different times as if they peaked together. In the first example it would give $150\ \Omega$ instead of $50\ \Omega$. Check: $Z$ can never be larger than $R + |X_L - X_C|$, and it equals $R$ only when $X_L = X_C$.

blocks.html: In a series RLC circuit, the impedance depends on frequency, because $X_L$ rises and $X_C$ falls. At one special frequency they cancel. There the circuit responds most strongly, the same way a swing goes highest when you push it at its natural rhythm. That is the natural frequency of the RLC circuit, now driven from outside.

Resonance at $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$: $X_L = X_C$, $Z = R$, the current is largest ($V/R$) and in step with the voltage.
Average power: $\bar{P} = I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi = I_{\text{rms}}^2R$, with power factor $\cos\phi = R/Z$. The sharpness of the resonance is measured by $Q = \omega_0L/R$.

Only the resistor turns electrical energy into heat. An inductor or capacitor stores energy for a quarter cycle and hands it back the next quarter: its current and voltage are $90^\circ$ apart, so their product averages to zero. For the whole circuit, only the part of the current in step with the voltage, $I\cos\phi$, delivers energy on average. And since $\cos\phi = R/Z$ and $V = IZ$, $IV\cos\phi = I^2R$. At resonance $\phi = 0$ and the circuit acts like the resistor alone.

blocks.title: At resonance
blocks.q: $R = 20\ \Omega$, $L = 0.10\ \text{H}$ and $C = 100\ \mu\text{F}$ are in series with a $10\ \text{V}$ rms source. Find the resonant frequency and the current and power there.

blocks.title: Off resonance
blocks.q: The same circuit is driven by $120\ \text{V}$ rms at $60\ \text{Hz}$. Find the power factor and the average power.

blocks.title: How sharp is the peak?
blocks.q: With the resistance lowered to $2.0\ \Omega$, find $Q$.
steps: The peak's width is about $f_0/Q \approx 3.18\ \text{Hz}$: a low-resistance circuit responds to a narrow band of frequencies, which is how a radio picks one station out of many.

blocks.html: "The power is always $I_{\text{rms}}V_{\text{rms}}$." That is true only when current and voltage are in step (a resistor, or any circuit at resonance). Otherwise part of the current only shuttles energy into the inductor or capacitor and back. In the second example, $IV$ overstates the power by about 15%. Check: the average power must equal $I_{\text{rms}}^2R$, the heat in the resistance.

blocks.html: Ampère's law says $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0I_{\text{enc}}$, where $I_{\text{enc}}$ is the current through any surface bounded by the path. Try it on a wire feeding a charging capacitor, and it breaks. Fixing it was Maxwell's great step, and it led straight to light.

Draw a circle around the wire near the capacitor. A flat disk bounded by that circle is pierced by the wire: $I_{\text{enc}} = I$. Now stretch the surface into a bag that passes between the plates, still bounded by the same circle. No charge crosses the gap, so $I_{\text{enc}} = 0$. Same path, two different answers: the law as written cannot be right. What does pass through the bag is a growing electric field. Between the plates $E = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0A}$, so $\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \varepsilon_0A\dfrac{dE}{dt} = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = I$: exactly the missing current.

The displacement current $I_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$ makes magnetic field just as a real current does: $$\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0\left(I_{\text{enc}} + \varepsilon_0\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\right).$$ In a charging capacitor, $I_d$ in the gap equals the current in the wires.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: An Ampère loop around a charging capacitor. With the displacement current counted, the loop gives the same answer whether its surface is pierced by the wire or passes through the gap.

blocks.title: How fast the field grows
blocks.q: A capacitor with circular plates of radius $10\ \text{cm}$ is charged by a current of $2.0\ \text{A}$. How fast does the field between the plates grow?

blocks.title: Magnetic field in the gap
blocks.q: For the same capacitor, find $B$ between the plates at $5.0\ \text{cm}$ from the axis, and at the plates' edge.
steps: The displacement current is spread evenly over the plates, so a circle of radius $r$ encloses $I\dfrac{r^2}{R^2}$.
At the edge, $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi R} = 4.00\ \text{μT}$, the same as next to the wire at that distance.

blocks.title: In terms of voltage
blocks.q: Show that the displacement current in a parallel-plate capacitor is $C\,dV/dt$.
steps: That is also $dq/dt$, the current in the wires.

blocks.html: "Charge flows across the gap of a charging capacitor." No charge crosses an ideal capacitor's gap: charge piles up on one plate and drains from the other. What fills the gap is a changing electric field, and that change acts like a current in producing a magnetic field. Check: if charge crossed, the capacitor would not charge at all.

Maxwell added this term in the 1860s, partly on grounds of consistency. It meant that a changing electric field makes a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field makes an electric field, so each can keep the other going through empty space: an electromagnetic wave. Heinrich Hertz made and detected such waves in the late 1880s.

blocks.html: Everything in this course rests on four laws. Each began as an experimental discovery: Coulomb's measurements of the electric force, the observation that magnets always have two poles, Faraday's induction, and Ampère's work on currents, completed by Maxwell's displacement current. Together with the Lorentz force, they describe all of classical electricity, magnetism and light.

head: Law
Equation
What it says
rows: Charges are sources of electric field; flux out of a closed surface counts the charge inside.
There are no magnetic charges: field lines never start or end.
A changing magnetic field makes a curling electric field.
Currents and changing electric fields make curling magnetic fields.
blocks.cap: Maxwell's equations in integral form.

blocks.html: Two laws are about flux through closed surfaces (the sources of $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$), and two are about circulation around loops (what makes the fields curl). Changing $\vec{B}$ makes $\vec{E}$; changing $\vec{E}$ makes $\vec{B}$. With $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ for how fields push charges, that is the whole theory.

Notice the near-symmetry. If magnetic charges existed, the second law would have a charge term like the first, and Faraday's law would gain a "magnetic current" like Ampère's. None has ever been found, despite careful searches, so the magnetic flux through every closed surface is zero: every field line that enters must leave. The two curl laws mirror each other with a sign difference, and that sign is what makes waves possible instead of runaway growth.

blocks.name: ph-magnetism
blocks.cap: A bar magnet's field lines form closed loops through the magnet. Around any closed surface, as many lines leave as enter. Break the magnet and each piece has both poles.

blocks.title: Closed-surface bookkeeping
blocks.q: The outward magnetic flux through the flat top of a closed cylinder is $5.0\ \text{mWb}$, and through its flat bottom $-2.0\ \text{mWb}$. What is the flux through its curved side?
steps: $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0$, so the three parts add to zero.
$5.0 + (-2.0) + \Phi_{\text{side}} = 0$, so $\Phi_{\text{side}} = -3.0\ \text{mWb}$ (more field enters through the side than leaves).

blocks.title: Which law?
blocks.q: Name the law behind each: (a) a transformer, (b) the field around the gap of a charging capacitor, (c) a lone north pole cannot exist, (d) the field outside a charged sphere is $kQ/r^2$.
steps: (a) Faraday's law: the changing flux of the primary induces an emf in the secondary.
(b) The Ampère–Maxwell law, through its displacement-current term.
(c) Gauss's law for magnetism. (d) Gauss's law.

blocks.title: Both kinds of current
blocks.q: A path encloses a wire carrying $2.0\ \text{A}$ and part of a capacitor gap where the electric flux grows at $1.0 \times 10^{11}\ \text{V·m/s}$. Find $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell}$.

blocks.html: "The magnetic flux through a closed surface can be nonzero, if the surface surrounds a magnet's north pole." That would require a lone magnetic charge. A real magnet's field lines run back through the magnet, so a surface around one end catches them coming out and going in. Check: any closed surface, anywhere, has zero net magnetic flux.

blocks.html: Maxwell's equations have a remarkable consequence. In empty space, with no charges and no currents, a changing $\vec{E}$ makes $\vec{B}$ and a changing $\vec{B}$ makes $\vec{E}$, so a disturbance can carry itself along. Maxwell computed its speed from two numbers measured with charges and magnets on a lab bench, and found the speed of light. You met electromagnetic waves in Physics 2; here is where they come from.

Take a wave moving along $x$, with $\vec{E}$ along $y$ and $\vec{B}$ along $z$. Apply Faraday's law to a thin rectangle in the $xy$-plane and the Ampère–Maxwell law to one in the $xz$-plane. In the limit of tiny rectangles they become, with partial derivatives, $$\frac{\partial E}{\partial x} = -\frac{\partial B}{\partial t}, \qquad -\frac{\partial B}{\partial x} = \mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial E}{\partial t}.$$ Differentiate the first by $x$ and the second by $t$ and combine: $\dfrac{\partial^2E}{\partial x^2} = \mu_0\varepsilon_0\dfrac{\partial^2E}{\partial t^2}$, the wave equation with speed $1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$. A wave $E = E_0\sin(kx - \omega t)$ in the first equation forces $B = (E_0/c)\sin(kx - \omega t)$: in step with $E$, and smaller by $c$.

In empty space electromagnetic waves travel at $$c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s},$$ with $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, in phase, and $E = cB$ at every point. The wave moves in the direction of $\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$.

blocks.cap: An electromagnetic wave: the electric and magnetic fields rise and fall together, at right angles, as the pattern moves along.

blocks.name: ph-spectrum
blocks.cap: All of these, radio to gamma rays, are the same kind of wave, moving at the same speed $c$ in empty space and differing only in wavelength.

blocks.title: The speed of light from lab constants
blocks.q: Compute $1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$ with $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T·m/A}$ and $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F/m}$.

blocks.title: The magnetic field of a wave
blocks.q: A light wave has an electric field amplitude of $30\ \text{V/m}$. Find its magnetic field amplitude.
steps: Small in tesla, but it carries as much energy as the electric field, as you will see next.

blocks.title: Finding directions
blocks.q: A wave travels along $+x$. At some instant $\vec{E}$ points along $+y$. Which way does $\vec{B}$ point?
steps: $\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$ must point along $+x$. Try $\vec{B}$ along $+z$: $\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{k} = \hat{\imath}$. That works.
So $\vec{B}$ points along $+z$; half a cycle later both fields reverse together.

blocks.html: "The electric and magnetic fields of light peak at different times, trading energy like an LC circuit." In a traveling wave they rise and fall together: $E = cB$ at every instant, as the step above showed. Each field is made by the other's change in space and time together, not by passing energy back and forth. Check: at a crest of $\vec{E}$, $\vec{B}$ is at a crest too.

blocks.html: Sunlight warms your skin: electromagnetic waves carry energy. Each field holds energy, $\tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E^2$ for the electric field and $B^2/2\mu_0$ for the magnetic one, and the wave carries both along at $c$. Less obviously, light also carries momentum, so it pushes on whatever absorbs or reflects it.

Average intensity (power per area): $$I = \tfrac{1}{2}c\varepsilon_0E_0^2 = \frac{E_0B_0}{2\mu_0},$$ flowing along the Poynting vector $\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0}\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$. Light carries momentum $p = U/c$, so it presses on a surface with pressure $I/c$ if absorbed and $2I/c$ if reflected straight back.

With $B = E/c$ and $c^2 = 1/(\mu_0\varepsilon_0)$, the magnetic energy density is $\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0} = \dfrac{E^2}{2\mu_0c^2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E^2$: exactly equal to the electric one. So the total is $u = \varepsilon_0E^2$, which averages to $\tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E_0^2$ over a cycle. This energy moves at $c$, so the energy crossing a square meter each second is $I = c\bar{u}$. For momentum: as light is absorbed, its electric field drives charges in the surface sideways, and the magnetic force $q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ on those moving charges points along the direction of travel. Working it through gives a push of $U/c$ for energy $U$ absorbed.

blocks.name: ph-wave
blocks.cap: The fields of a light wave: energy is stored equally in $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ and flows along $\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$, the direction the wave moves.

blocks.title: Sunlight's fields
blocks.q: Sunlight above Earth's atmosphere delivers about $1360\ \text{W/m}^2$ (NASA). Treating it as one wave, find $E_0$ and $B_0$.
steps: $B_0 = E_0/c = 3.37\ \text{μT}$, much less than Earth's own magnetic field.

blocks.title: Pressure and a solar sail
blocks.q: Find the radiation pressure of that sunlight on an absorbing surface and on a mirror, and the force on an $800\ \text{m}^2$ reflecting sail.
steps: Sail: $F = (9.07 \times 10^{-6})(800) = 7.25\ \text{mN}$. Tiny, but it never stops, and in space nothing slows the sail down.

blocks.title: Spreading from a source
blocks.q: A lamp radiates $100\ \text{W}$ of light evenly in all directions. Find the intensity and $E_0$ at $2.0\ \text{m}$.
steps: The power spreads over a sphere: $I = \dfrac{100}{4\pi(2.0)^2} = 1.99\ \text{W/m²}$.
$E_0 = \sqrt{2I/(c\varepsilon_0)} = 38.7\ \text{V/m}$. Intensity falls as $1/r^2$, so $E_0$ falls as $1/r$.

blocks.html: "Absorbed and reflected light push equally hard." The push equals the light's change in momentum. Absorbed light arrives with momentum $p$ and ends with none: change $p$. Reflected light leaves with $-p$: change $2p$. So a mirror feels twice the force, like a ball that bounces off a wall compared with one that sticks. Check the formulas: $I/c$ for absorption, $2I/c$ for reflection.
